Affiliation

1 Introduction

1.1 Motivation

In Electronic Design and Automation (EDA) for Integrated Circuits (ICs), a schematic presents an abstraction in comparison to the layout that will eventually be taped-out and fabricated by the semiconductor foundry.

While in the schematic, a connection between device terminals is seen as an equipotential, the stacked geometries in a specific layout introduce parasitic effects, which can be thought of additional resistors, capacitors (and inductors), not modeled by and missing in the original schematic.

To be able to simulate these effects, a parasitic extraction tool (PEX) is used, to extract a netlist from the layout, which represents the original schematic (created from the layout active and passive elements) augmented with the additional parasitic devices.

1.3 About KLayout-PEX

KLayout is an open source VLSI layout viewer and editor.

KLayout-PEX (short KPEX) is a PEX tool, well integrated with KLayout by using its API.

There are multiple PEX engines supported, currently:

  • FasterCap integration (field solver engine)
  • FastCap2 integration (field solver engine, selected with --fastcap)
  • MAGIC integration (wrapper calling magic)
  • Analytical 2.5D engine (parasitic concepts and formulas of MAGIC, implemented using KLayout methods)
Tip

KPEX tool source code itself is made publicly available on GitHub (follow this link) and shared under the GPL-3.0 license.

KPEX documentation source code is made publicly available on GitHub (follow this link) and shared under the Apache-2.0 license.

Please feel free to create issues and/or submit pull requests on GitHub to fix errors and omissions!

The production of the tool and this document would be impossible without these (and many more) great open-source software products: KLayout, FasterCap, FastCap2, MAGIC, Palace, Elmer, OpenRCX, KQCircuits, protobuf, Quarto, Python, ngspice, Numpy, Scipy, Matplotlib, Git, Docker, Ubuntu, Linux…

1.4 Status

Caution

Currently, KPEX is developed as a Python prototype, using the KLayout Python API. This allows for a faster development cycle during the current prototyping phase.

Eventually, critical parts will be re-implemented in Rust and parallelized to improve performance.

Warning

KPEX is experimental. Extraction and consistency checks do not establish calibrated accuracy for every device or layout.

RC includes coupling capacitances. There is no separate RCC value for --mode.

1.5 Installation

Generally, KPEX is deployed using PyPi (Python Package Index), install via:

pip3 install --upgrade klayout-pex

kpex --version   # check the installed version 
kpex --help      # this will help with command line arguments

As for the dependencies, there are multiple options available.

1.5.1 Option 1: Using IIC-OSIC-TOOLS Docker Image

We provide a comprehensive, low entry barrier Docker image that comes pre-installed with most relevant open source ASIC tools, as well as the open PDKs. This is a pre-compiled Docker image which allows to do circuit design on a virtual machine on virtually any type of computing equipment (personal PC, Raspberry Pi, cloud server) on various operating systems (Windows, macOS, Linux).

For further information please look at the Docker Hub page and for detailed instructions at the IIC-OSIC-TOOLS GitHub page.

WarningLinux

In this document, we assume that users have a basic knowledge of Linux and how to operate it using the terminal (shell). If you are not yet familiar with Linux (which is basically a must when doing integrated circuit design as many tools are only available on Linux), then please check out a Linux introductory course or tutorial online, there are many resources available.

A summary of important Linux shell commands is provided in IIC-JKU Linux Cheatsheet.

1.5.2 Option 2: Standalone Installation

  • KLayout layout tool:
    • is mandatory for all engines (besides the MAGIC-wrapper)
    • get the latest pre-built package version
    • or follow the build instructions
  • FasterCap engine:
    • optional, required to run the FasterCap engine
    • either compile your own version from the GitHub repository
    • or use precompiled versions available at https://github.com/martinjankoehler/FasterCap/releases
  • MAGIC-wrapper engine:
    • optional, required to run the MAGIC-wrapper engine
    • use MAGIC 8.3.693 or newer for the corrected sidewall counting (see Section 5.4)
    • Follow the installation instructions at the GitHub repository
  • Skywater sky130A PDK:
    • optional, for now, KPEX technology specific files are deployed within the klayout-pex Python package
    • pip3 install --upgrade ciel (install PDK package manager)
    • ciel ls-remote --pdk sky130A (retrieve available PDK releases
      • for example PRE-RELEASE 0c1df35fd535299ea1ef74d1e9e15dedaeb34c32 (2024.12.11))
    • ciel enable --pdk sky130A 0c1df35fd535299ea1ef74d1e9e15dedaeb34c32 (install a PDK version)
    • PDK files now have been installed under $HOME/.volare/sky130A
  • IHP SG13G2 PDK:
    • optional, for now, KPEX technology specific files are deployed within the klayout-pex Python package
    • pip3 install --upgrade ciel (install PDK package manager)
    • ciel ls-remote --pdk ihp-sg13g2 (retrieve available PDK releases
      • for example PRE-RELEASE cb7daaa8901016cf7c5d272dfa322c41f024931f (2025.07.18))
    • ciel enable --pdk ihp-sg13g2 cb7daaa8901016cf7c5d272dfa322c41f024931f (install a PDK version)
    • PDK files now have been installed under $HOME/.volare/ihp-sg13g2

1.5.3 Checking Tool Versions

The Python package requires klayout>=0.30.12. KLayout 0.30.13 is recommended for terminal-lookup performance, neighborhood-visitor memory fixes and resistance-extraction crash fixes. The recommendation is a warning, so an environment still shipping 0.30.12 can run.

The CLI checks the Python module and the executable separately when both are used. Updating one does not update the other. An LVS-database-only extraction can use the module without the executable. The runtime table lists the version found, the required range and the recommended range.

An unrecognized tool version is reported as unchecked. warn and off do not repair the numerical or performance defects of an older executable.

For --magic, KPEX 0.9.0 requires MAGIC 8.3.693 or newer, which removes an extra sidewall halving. Pure --2.5D extraction does not require a MAGIC executable. The remaining multi-polygon device-terminal limitation is separate from the recommendation to upgrade KLayout and is not resolved by installing 0.30.13.

1.5.4 Useful tools: meshlab

For previewing generated 3D geometries, representing the input to FasterCap, we recommend installing MeshLab. The generated STL-files are located at output/<design>/Geometries/*.stl.

2 First Steps

  • The command line tool kpex is used to trigger the parasitic extraction flow from the terminal.
  • Get extraction help with kpex extract --help
  • Inspect or reduce netlists with the separate netlist command
  • Inspect interchange files with the separate pex25d command

2.1 Example Layouts

Example layouts are included in the testdata/designs subdirectory of the KLayout-PEX source code:

git clone https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex.git
cd klayout-pex

# for sky130A
find testdata/designs/sky130A -name "*.gds.gz"

# for IHP SG13G2
find testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2 -name "*.gds.gz"

2.2 Running KPEX/2.5D

From the KPEX source directory:

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode RC --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz \
  --out-netlist nfet_li1-rc.spice

CC extracts capacitances with one equipotential node per net. R resolves the wire resistance, and RC adds the coupling capacitances to that distributed network. --blackbox y retains recognized device models instead of extracting their modeled capacitor interiors. Select it explicitly because the current prototype defaults to whiteboxing for development.

Use --schematic to follow an existing testbench interface (Section 6.4). RC enables consistency failures by default; Section 7 explains the diagnostics and the additional checks that can be requested.

Each run directory contains kpex_result.json, which records the output paths, warnings, errors and final status. A written netlist can coexist with failed checks, so inspect the exit status and diagnostics before simulation.

2.3 Generating PEX25D

kpex pex25d generates a PEX25D geometry and material description without running a solver. It is separate from the analytical KPEX/2.5D engine. See Section 10.1 for the format specification, benefits, and standalone tools.

From the KLayout-PEX source directory:

kpex pex25d --pdk sky130A --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/nmos_diode2/nmos_diode2.gds.gz \
  --out-file nmos_diode2.pex25d \
  --out-scene nmos_diode2.pex25d.scene.pb

The .pex25d file contains the text representation. The .pex25d.scene.pb file contains the resolved protobuf scene, including absolute layer heights and terminal intersections. Generation runs the reference validator by default; diagnostics determine the exit code even when output files have been written.

Use the standalone tool to inspect or validate an artifact:

pex25d show nmos_diode2.pex25d
pex25d validate nmos_diode2.pex25d --strict

For a complete, hand-written file that can be validated and exported without layout generation, use the downloadable example in Section 10.1.4. Terminal semantics and the current state of KLayout-generated terminals are explained in Section 10.1.5.7.

2.4 Running the KPEX/FasterCap engine

Preconditions:

  • klayout-pex was installed, see Section 1.5
  • FasterCap was installed, see Section 1.5
Note

Normally, devices with SPICE (Nagel 1975) simulation models (e.g. like MOM-capacitors1 in the sky130A PDK) are ignored (“blackboxed”) during parasitic extraction.

kpex has an option --blackbox n to allow extraction of those devices (whiteboxing), which can be useful during development (during the prototype phase, whiteboxing is actually the default setting, so please use --blackbox y to explicitly configure blackboxing).

Let’s try the following:

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --blackbox n --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz
Note

This will report an error that we have not activated one or more engines, and list the available engines:

Argument Description
--fastercap Run kpex/FasterCap engine
--2.5D Run kpex/2.5D engine
--magic Run MAGIC engine

Now, to run the FasterCap engine (might take a couple of minutes):

kpex extract --pdk sky130A --blackbox n --fastercap --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz

Within the output directory (defaults to output), KPEX creates a subdirectory Geometries, containing STL-files that provide a preview of the FasterCap input geometries. Use MeshLab (see Section 1.5.4) to open and preview those files:

ls -d output/cap_vpp_04*/Geometries/*.stl
Tip
  • Open the *.stl files in MeshLab
  • Use the eye buttons to hide and show each file/mesh
  • Use the align tool (“A” in the toolbar) to assign different colors
  • Start by showing only on the conductors (files named cond_*.stl)
  • Then try showing different dielectrics (files named diel_*.stl), to see how they surround the conductors.

In the log file, we see the output of FasterCap including the Maxwell capacitance matrix:

Capacitance matrix is:
Dimension 3 x 3
g1_VSUBS  5.2959e-09 -4.46971e-10 -1.67304e-09
g2_C1  -5.56106e-10 1.5383e-08 -1.47213e-08
g3_C0  -1.69838e-09 -1.48846e-08 1.64502e-08

KPEX interprets this matrix and prints a CSV netlist, which can be pasted into a spreadsheet application:

Device;Net1;Net2;Capacitance [fF]
Cext_0_1;VSUBS;C1;0.5
Cext_0_2;VSUBS;C0;1.69
Cext_1_2;C1;C0;14.8
Cext_1_1;C1;VSUBS;0.08

In addition, a SPICE netlist is generated.

2.5 Running the KPEX/MAGIC engine

Preconditions:

  • klayout-pex was installed, see Section 1.5
  • magic was installed, see Section 1.5

The MAGIC section of kpex extract --help describes the arguments and their defaults. Important arguments:

  • --magicrc: specify location of the magicrc file
  • --gds: path to the GDS input layout
  • --magic: enable magic engine
kpex extract --pdk sky130A --magic --gds \
  testdata/designs/sky130A/*/cap_vpp_04p4x04p6_l1m1m2_noshield.gds.gz

3 Choosing and describing PDKs

A PDK2 supplies more than a list of GDS layer numbers. KPEX needs to know which shapes conduct, how they connect, what surrounds them in three dimensions, and which part of a device is already represented by its circuit model. The technology definition keeps these choices together, while the extraction algorithms remain independent of the PDK.

3.1 Choosing the process variant

--pdk selects a complete combination of extraction deck, layer stack, parasitic tables and device mappings. Choose the variant used by the layout and its simulation models. Changing only a top-metal name cannot turn one stack into another.

The older spelling ihp_sg13g2 remains an alias for ihp-sg13g2. Use the hyphenated spelling in new commands and scripts. The other three spellings in Table 3 are the accepted identifiers, including their capitalization.

This is a list of extraction configurations, not a claim that every device of each PDK has a simulation mapping. An extracted device without a supported mapping produces an error instead of a guessed model call.

3.2 Forming nets and identifying layers

The PEX extraction decks use KLayout’s LVS facilities to recognize devices and establish connectivity. This step produces the flat netlist and the named, net-associated polygons in the LVSDB. Comparing that result with a schematic is a separate operation.

The deck and technology definition must agree on the meaning of each computed layer. A name alone is insufficient: a piece of drawn metal may have a different role inside a capacitor than outside it.

There are three identities to keep distinct:

  • The computed layer identifies polygons produced by the extraction deck, including their net and device role
  • The original layer selects the physical layer’s parasitic coefficients
  • The process layer selects its position and material environment in the three-dimensional stack

For example, the ihp-sg13g2 deck splits drawn Metal5 into ordinary routing, MIM3 bottom-plate and device-related regions. All use coefficients keyed by Metal5, but their process layers distinguish metal under the MIM dielectric from ordinary metal.

The computed-layer kind also specifies whether a region is ordinary conductor, a modeled capacitor plate, a resistor region, or device-internal geometry. This is why removing a capacitor from the parasitic sum does not necessarily remove its plates from shielding or from coupling to other nets. See Section 6 and the section on excluding parts of the layout for the extraction choices.

When adding a deck, assign stable names with name(layer, name). Keep the named device regions and the technology’s layer identities consistent. A pin label, a device plate and a physical routing layer are different contracts even when they originate from the same drawn GDS layer.

3.3 Keeping technology data together

The technology definition uses a Protocol Buffers schema and is distributed as JSON. Its parts answer different questions:

The main schema is tech.proto. It incorporates process_stack.proto, process_parasitics.proto, device_models.proto and the substrate definition. These schemas define the data contract; the generated JSON contains the values for a particular variant.

Changing a dielectric height does not automatically refit the KPEX/2.5D coefficients. The stack and tables are separate inputs. This matters when comparing a three-dimensional solve with the table-based engine: both must describe the same intended physical process.

3.4 Describing the process stack

For 3D solvers, like the KPEX/FasterCap engine, 3D information about the dimensions (e.g. z-offset and thickness) of metal layers is required, as well as the dielectrics in-between.

The sky130A stack illustrates why a list of metal heights alone is not enough: several different dielectric profiles surround the same conductor.

The stack distinguishes conductors from the material around them:

  • Metals such as poly, metal1 and metal5 have a thickness and a bottom height relative to the substrate
  • Contacts and vias, such as licon and via1, connect conductors on adjacent levels
  • Sidewall dielectrics, such as IOX and SPNIT, specify lateral width and height above metal
  • Conformal dielectrics, such as LINT and TOPNIT, specify thickness above metal, beside it and in the field
  • Simple dielectrics, such as PSG and NILD2, fill the remaining region between levels

The relative permittivity \(k\) belongs to each dielectric. A stack may therefore contain several dielectric boundaries around one piece of metal. The schematic labels above and the technology’s physical-layer names need not be identical; their correspondence is explicit in the technology definition.

The schema excerpt below shows how these relationships are expressed:

  • ProcessStackInfo.layers orders the layers of the stack
  • MetalLayer.z locates the metal bottom relative to the substrate
  • MetalLayer.contact_above describes the contact to the next conductor
  • A dielectric reference identifies the layer or profile it wraps
  • Wrapping can be nested: SPNIT wraps IOX, which wraps poly
message ProcessStackInfo {

    enum LayerType { …
        LAYER_TYPE_SIMPLE_DIELECTRIC = 50;
        LAYER_TYPE_CONFORMAL_DIELECTRIC = 60;
        LAYER_TYPE_SIDEWALL_DIELECTRIC = 70;
        LAYER_TYPE_METAL = 80;
    }

    message Contact { // Contact/Via
        string name = 1;
        string layer_below = 9;
        string metal_above = 10;
        double thickness = 20;

        double width = 30;
        double spacing = 31;
        double border = 32;
    } 
    …
    message SimpleDielectricLayer { // Simple dielectric
        double dielectric_k = 10;
        string reference = 30;
    }

    message ConformalDielectricLayer { // Conformal dielectric
        double dielectric_k = 10;
        double thickness_over_metal = 20;
        double thickness_where_no_metal = 21;
        double thickness_sidewall = 22;
        string reference = 30;
    }

    message SidewallDielectricLayer { // Sidewall dielectric
        double dielectric_k = 10;
        double height_above_metal = 20; // might be 0 if none
        double width_outside_sidewall = 21;
        string reference = 30;
    }

    message MetalLayer { // Metal
        double z = 1;          // z-offset in µm (of layer bottom), above substrate
        double thickness = 2;  // thickness in µm
        Contact contact_above = 40;
    }

    message LayerInfo {
        string name = 1;
        LayerType layer_type = 2;
        oneof parameters { …
            SimpleDielectricLayer simple_dielectric_layer = 12;
            ConformalDielectricLayer conformal_dielectric_layer = 13;
            SidewallDielectricLayer sidewall_dielectric_layer = 14;
            MetalLayer metal_layer = 15;
        }
    }

    repeated LayerInfo layers = 100;
}

3.4.1 Planar passivation over gf180mcuD

The top surface is an instructive example of why the reference of a dielectric matters. For the selected 1P5M/11KA/MIM-B stack, the maintained cross-section drawing gives the oxide surface relative to the bottom of Metal5.

Metal5 is \(1.1925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) thick. The planar oxide surface is \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above its bottom, leaving \(1.2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) of oxide over the metal. A \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) nitride layer sits above that surface. Its relative permittivity is \(7\), while the oxide uses \(4\), as recorded in the maintained dielectric table.

The technology expresses these planar surfaces using two wrapped dielectric profiles:

  • pass wraps Metal5, with \(1.2\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above metal and \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) in the field
  • sin wraps pass, with \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) above the oxide and \(2.6925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) in the field
  • Both use zero sidewall growth, preserving flat interfaces over the gap

The field height of sin includes the oxide height because it is measured from the wrapped profile’s bottom. Treating it as only \(0.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) would place nitride near the bottom of the gap instead of above the oxide.

The general dielectric table lists \(2.3\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) for the 11KA oxide. KPEX uses the detailed cross-section’s \(2.3925\,\mu\mathrm{m}\) consistently with the metal thickness from the same drawing. This is an explicit source choice, not a fitted capacitance correction. The maintained community PDK repository is the source of these dimensions.

3.5 Interpreting parasitic coefficients

The capacitance tables are a compact model of geometry. Each family has different dimensions because it multiplies a different geometric quantity. Mixing their units can yield plausible-looking values with the wrong scale.

For an overlap area \(A\) and area coefficient \(c_A\), the model contribution is \(C=c_A A\). The coefficient is per square micrometre. A perimeter or fringe coefficient instead multiplies a length, and the fringe calculation supplies the fraction left after distance limits and shielding.

The sidewall coefficient has a different form. For two facing parallel edges of length \(L\), gap \(s\) and fitted offset \(o\), the table convention is

\[ C_{\mathrm{pair}}=b\,\frac{L}{s_{\mathrm{eff}}}, \qquad s_{\mathrm{eff}}=\max(s+o,s/2). \]

The ratio of lengths is dimensionless, so \(b\) is in attofarads. It is not an area density or a capacitance per micrometre. A negative fitted offset is allowed; the lower bound on effective separation prevents a zero or negative denominator for positive gaps. For a varying gap, integrate this density along the edge instead of substituting an average gap.

This equation defines the full-pair coefficient convention. In KPEX 0.9.0, each of the two directed visits contributes half, so their sum follows this law. Earlier versions applied an extra halving. The coefficient must not be doubled to compensate for that older behavior: contribution counting and physical table values are separate parts of the model.

The stored capacitance units are attofarads; extraction reports commonly use femtofarads, with \(1000\,\mathrm{aF}=1\,\mathrm{fF}\). Resistance tables use milliohms per square for sheets and milliohms per contact or via cut.

3.5.1 Direction and physical consistency

A side-overlap row from an edge on Metal1 toward a conductor on Metal2 describes a different geometric contribution from a row in the reverse direction. These coefficients can differ without violating reciprocal capacitance: the final coupling of a node pair includes the applicable contributions, not a choice of just one directional row.

Physical comparisons need the whole environment:

  • Equal conductor spacing and equal dielectric material give the same parallel-plate density
  • Equal gaps alone do not imply equal sidewall fits when height above substrate or nearby conductors differs
  • Variants with identical complete conductor and dielectric surroundings should not acquire different values solely from renaming layers
  • A changed fit can alter both \(b\) and \(o\), so compare its predicted capacitance over the relevant gaps

Shared lower-layer dimensions do not make two complete stacks identical. Different upper metals or passivation can change the fitted capacitance of those lower conductors.

The tables are based in part on the extraction sections of MAGIC technology files. Importing those values does not import MAGIC’s layer classification, device recognition, shielding or grid rounding. Agreement of one test pattern therefore does not establish agreement for every layout.

3.6 Mapping extracted devices to circuit models

An LVS device class is not necessarily the model name or primitive type expected by a simulator. The mapping declares:

  • The instance prefix, such as M or X
  • The target model or subcircuit name
  • The order of its terminals
  • Which parameters are exported, their names and their conversion factors
  • Fixed parameters, such as an RF-mode selector

For example, the ihp-sg13* LVS class rfnmos maps to an X call of sg13_lv_nmos with rfmode=1. Its terminal order is D, G, S, B. The mapping supplies this information explicitly instead of assuming that every four-terminal device is a native MOS model.

Lengths and areas also need an explicit contract. An ihp-sg13* LVS length stored in micrometres is exported to the model in metres using lvs_parameter_factor=1e-6. An area needs the square of that length factor. A mapping may give schematic_parameter_factors for different SPICE prefixes: a native M device read with geometry scaling and an X wrapper parameter do not have identical unit semantics. These factors describe the PDK model interface; they are separate from the netlist’s .option scale setting.

For symmetric area/perimeter models, the mapping can recover equivalent rectangle sides from area \(A\) and perimeter \(P\). The sides solve \(wl=A\) and \(2(w+l)=P\). This preserves those two geometric quantities without claiming to recover the original orientation. It is unsuitable for a transistor or varactor whose model depends differently on width and length.

3.6.1 Independent capacitance references

A KIND_METAL_CAPACITOR mapping can also contain capacitance_references. These describe the nominal mutual capacitance of a particular unordered terminal pair. They are used by the device-capacitance check, not to tune the extraction result.

Each reference states:

  • Two terminal names whose local plates can be compared
  • A capacitance expression in farads, using mapped model parameters
  • Optional derived parameters and a validity condition
  • A source and its nominal assumptions

The instance multiplier belongs in the reference exactly once. A validity condition restricts the expression to the supported geometry; it is not permission to extrapolate outside the model’s domain. The check evaluates the recorded expression without running a simulator or searching arbitrary SPICE libraries.

The bundled references currently cover cap_cmomf and cap_cmomi in ihp-sg13*. The cap_cmomf reference uses nominal area density and the selected metal count. The cap_cmomi reference additionally reflects its discrete finger array and feed option. Their provenance is pinned to the device model sources.

These references do not include process-corner or mismatch variation. Some densities are estimates or derived from a sibling stack, as stated in each reference’s description. A ratio between extracted and nominal capacitance helps find a discrepancy; it does not by itself identify which model is physically correct. Unlisted device pairs have no such reference check.

3.7 Updating technology data

The built-in definitions are produced by Python generators4. The generated JSON and Python schema modules are packaged in the distribution, but are not committed source files in the code repository. Editing an installed JSON file is temporary: a rebuild or package upgrade replaces it.

For a source change:

  1. Change the relevant PDK generator, with the source revision and the reason for the choice
  2. Run ./gen_tech_pb.sh from the klayout-pex checkout to regenerate the schema modules and all built-in JSON definitions
  3. Compare the resulting tables by physical layer and coefficient family
  4. Check the affected geometries and sibling variants before interpreting changed extraction values

The generators contain deliberate projections, not only verbatim copies of upstream tables. Diffusion rows may be shared between extracted implant or tap regions. MIM plates retain their model-derived plate coupling while surrounding parasitics come from other rows. Resistance overrides have their own sources. A table refresh must preserve these distinctions and show changed values for review.

The nominal sky130A and gf180mcuD tables in KPEX 0.9.0 follow the maintained open-pdks extraction sources. The ihp-sg13g2 and ihp-sg13cmos5l tables use the corrected extraction fits at 14b1ab8. These refreshes preserve the diffusion and MIM derivations and resistance overrides. They do not change the independent device-model references. Automatic calibration and selectable capacitance corners are not available in 0.9.0.

3.8 Inspecting the generated definitions

The previews below contain the generated technology definitions from klayout-pex 0.9.0, including the device mappings, gf180mcuD passivation and refreshed nominal capacitance tables. They show the data packaged with that release; your local installation may contain a different version.

To inspect the data actually installed, locate klayout_pex_protobuf beside the klayout_pex package in site-packages5. Its filenames use the PDK identifiers from Table 3, followed by _tech.pb.json.

  • sky130A
  • gf180mcuD
  • ihp-sg13g2
  • ihp-sg13cmos5l




















































4 KPEX/FasterCap Engine


FasterCap is a 3D and 2D parallel capacitance field solver, inspired by FastCap2. https://www.fastfieldsolvers.com/fastercap.htm


Starting from an input layout (e.g. GDS file) and a process stack-up (part of the Section 3.3), KPEX creates input geometries for FasterCap. After running FasterCap, the Maxwell capacitance matrix is parsed and interpreted to obtain the parasitic capacitances.


See Section 2.4 to get started with a first extraction example.









4.1 3D Input Geometries







The FasterCap input files and their format is documented in (Di Lorenzo 2019), a PDF version of the Windows-specific *.chm file is available at https://github.com/martinjankoehler/FasterCap/tree/master/doc/pdf.


KPEX generates 3D input geometries:


    

  • *.lst file: Main input file

      

    • defines dielectric instances
      • 

    • defines conductor instances
      • 

    • each instance refers to a *.geo file
      • 

    • 

  • *.geo files: Defines single geometry

      

    • defines shapes (e.g. triangles)
      • 

    • Each shape has a reference point to define inside/outsides
      • 

    • 












4.2 Example: MOM Capacitor







Figure 4 depicts the MOM capacitor from Section 2.4.


The corresponding schematic representation of Figure 5 contains 3 conductors (\(N_1\), \(N_2\) and \(N_3\)), and coupling capacitances:


    

  • Capacitances between conductors: \(C_{ij} \text{ where } i \ne j\)

      

    • \(C_{23}\) is the capacitance “intended” by the MOM designer
      • 

    • 

  • Capacitances between conductors and ground: \(C_{ii}\)
    • 




















4.3 Output Maxwell Capacitance Matrix


A Maxwell capacitance matrix (Maxwell 1873) provides the relation between voltages on a set of conductors and the charges on these conductors, as described by the FasterCap author in the white paper (Di Lorenzo 2023).


FasterCap log output prints the Maxwell capacitance matrix (one for each iteration/refinement).







    

  • Matrix Properties:

      

    • Scaling: units have to be divided by \(10^{-6}\)
      • 

    • rows and columns are the same (list of net names)
      • 

    • Row Cells:

        

      • off diagonals cells contains the coupling between row/col nets (times \(-1\))
        • 

      • diagonal cells contains the sum of the absolute values of all other cells in the row
        • 

      • 

    • Matrix Symmetry:

        

      • in theory (ideal world), the matrix would be symmetric
        • 

      • in practice it’s not
        

        • 

      • therefore FastCap2 did average the off-diagonals
        • 

      • FasterCap does not average, so it’s done as part of KPEX
        • 

      • 

    • 
















5 KPEX/MAGIC Engine


This engine is merely just a wrapper around magic, which prepares a TCL script that opens the layout file and starts MAGIC’s PEX flow. See Section 2.5 to get started with a first extraction example.


The following chapter will illustrate concepts of the parasitic extraction done in MAGIC, also motivated by the fact that the engine in Section 6 will be based on those. Major parts of this illustration, the figures and concepts are based on work done by MAGIC maintainer Tim Edwards, especially his talk from FSiC conference 2022 (Edwards 2022) and a (conceptual follow-up) ChipsAlliance meeting on April 4, 2023, see (Edwards 2023b) and (Edwards 2023a). In addition, code review and debugging of the MAGIC codebase was performed.




5.1 MAGIC database units


    

  • To convert between MAGIC database units and \(\mu m\), a scaling factor \(\alpha\) is used, so that \(L_{\mu m} = \frac{L_{dbu}}{\alpha}\)
    • 

  • E.g. for sky130A, \(\alpha = 200.0\)
    • 







5.2 Types of Parasitic Capacitances


MAGIC models multiple types of capacitances:


    

  • Substrate Overlap: Overlap area of a metal with the substrate
    • 

  • Substrate Fringing: Sidewall of a metal fringes out to substrate
    • 

  • Sidewall Capacitance: Coupling between adjacent sidewalls on the same layer
    • 

  • Overlap Capacitance: Overlap on different metal layers
    • 

  • Fringe Capacitance (“Side Overlap”): Sidewall of a metal fringes out other metal layers
    • 







5.3 Substrate Capacitance




    

  • Overlapping area: \[
C_{area} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\]
    • 

  • Fringe (“Perimeter”): \[
C_{fringe\,to\,substrate} = \text{perimeter} * C_{perim} = (2l + 2w)*C_{perim}
\]
    • 

  • Coefficients like \(C_{perim}\) are part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    • 







5.4 Sidewall Capacitance




\[
C_{sidewall} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{s} * \text{sidewall area}  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\] \[
\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,= \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{s} * t * l  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m * \mu m\right]
\] \[
C_{sidewall} = \frac{C_{sidewall\,coeff}}{s} * l \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m} * \mu m\right]
\]


The coefficient describes the coupling between the two facing sidewalls, but MAGIC walks every edge, so each of the two edges contributes half of it:


\[
C_{sidewall\,per\,edge} = \frac{1}{2} * \frac{C_{sidewall\,coeff}}{s} * l
\]




    

  • Coefficients are part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    • 

  • Layer thickness \(t\) is normally multiplied into the coefficient
    • 

  • Foundry tables give constant coefficient referenced to \(s = 1\)
    • 















WarningCount the sidewall pair once







The sidewall coefficient describes the full pair. Half belongs to each directed edge visit. A second halving of the already weighted coefficient makes the pair too small by a factor of two.


MAGIC 8.3.693 removes that extra halving during final technology processing. The earlier interpretation that revisions before 8.3.679 simply counted the pair twice was incorrect. The upstream correction explains the two sites that applied the factor.


KPEX 0.9.0 restores the full pair value for both constant and sloped gaps. Updating the physical coefficient tables is a separate change: multiplying all extraction results by two would also alter overlap and fringe contributions, which are not affected by this counting correction.










5.5 Overlap Capacitance


    

  • Overlapping area: \[
C_{area} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{F}{\mu m^2} * \mu m^2\right]
\]
    • 












5.6 Fringe Capacitance







    

  • Causing sidewall (its bottom edge depicted red)
    • 

  • Assume: Field is bounded by fringe halo (e.g. \(8\, \mu m\) away from edge)
    • 

  • Fractions of fringe goes to metal1 or substrate
    • 








    

  • Multiplier \(\alpha\) (comes from tech files: overlap table)

      

    • determines how quickly fringe capacitance drops with increasing distance
      • 

    • \(\alpha\) is related to distance \(d\) between layers
      • 

    • \(\alpha\) is proportional to \(C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}}= \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area}\)
      
(for fixed value of area \(1\, \mu m^2\)) 
      • 

    • 

  • Fringe Fractions:

      

    • \(\text{frac}_{metal1} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}*x)\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{sub} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}*(\text{halo}-x))\)
      • 

    • \(\tfrac{2}{\pi}\) is multiplied because of scaling to interval \([0.0,\,1.0]\), as \(\text{atan}(\infty)=\tfrac{\pi}{2}\)
      • 

    • 

  • Overlap capacitance:

      

    • \(C_{overlap} = \frac{\epsilon_{si} * K}{d} * \text{area} \,\,\,\,\,\,\,\,(\text{with area}=1 \mu m^2)\)
      • 

    • 

  • Coupling capacitance \(metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2\):

      

    • \(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2} = \alpha_{scalefac} * C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}}\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{metal1} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow metal2}*x)\)
      • 

    • \(\text{effective length} = \text{edge length} * \text{frac}_{metal1}\)
      • 

    • \(C_{fringe_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}} = \text{effective length} * C_{sideoverlap_{metal2 \rightarrow metal1}}\)
      • 

    • 

  • Coupling capacitance \(metal1 \leftrightarrow sub\):

      

    • \(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub} = \alpha_{scalefac} * C_{overlap_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub}}\)
      • 

    • \(\text{frac}_{sub} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha_{metal1 \leftrightarrow sub}*(\text{halo}-x))\)
      • 

    • \(\text{effective length} = \text{edge length} * \text{frac}_{sub}\)
      • 

    • \(C_{fringe_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}} = \text{effective length} * C_{sideoverlap_{metal2 \rightarrow sub}}\)
      • 

    • 








    

  • Partial side overlap

      

    • In case there is only a partial side overlap, the non-existing near fraction is subtracted from the far fraction
      • 

    • \(metal1\) wire is offset, starts at \(x_{near}\)
      • 

    • \(metal1\) ends at \(x_{far}\)
      • 

    • 








    

  • \(\text{frac}_{near} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha*x_{near})\)
    • 

  • \(\text{frac}_{far} = \tfrac{2}{\pi} * \text{atan}(\alpha*x_{far})\)
    • 

  • \(\text{frac} = \text{frac}_{far}-\text{frac}_{near}\)
    • 







5.7 Shielding Effects












Note, given an analyzed sidewall (edge in 2D), lateral fringe shielding


    

  • is caused by opposing shapes on the same layer

      

    • even by the same polygon
      • 

    • by other polygons (same net)
      • 

    • by other polygons (different net) — this is what we also look at when analyzing sidewall coupling
      • 

    • 

  • will shield the fringing to the lower layers, i.e. in Figure 7 the coupling between the two shapes is the same in the above and below cases
    • 












5.8 Parasitic Resistance


Magic constructs a graph of resistors between nodes


    

  • device terminals
    • 

  • pins
    • 

  • junctions (vias or branching on the same metal layer)
    • 









5.8.1 Wire resistance


    

  • Given a wire with length \(l\) and height \(h\), the basic formula is \[
R_{wire} = \frac{l}{h} * R_{coeff}  \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[ \frac{\mu m}{\mu m} * mΩ\right]
\]
    • 

  • Coefficient \(R_{coeff}\) is part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)
    

      

    • defined for every metal layer
      • 

    • in \(mΩ\) for \(1\,{\mu m}^2\)
      • 

    • Coefficient already includes the thickness aspect of the layer, so the formula works in 2D
      • 

    • 







5.8.2 Via resistance







    

  • Given

      

    • drawn via in the layout, with width \(w\) and height \(h\)
      • 

    • design rules defined for each via layer:

        

      • via width \(viawidth\)
        • 

      • \(spacing\) between vias (in case of a via array)
        • 

      • \(border\) on each side of the via
        • 

      • 

    • 

  • MAGIC interpretation of the via drawing

      

    • determine number of vias in \(x\) and \(y\) direction, i.e. \(n_x\) and \(n_y\)
      • 

    • if \(x\) and \(y\) dimensions are below the minimum size, MAGIC counts 1 via in each direction
      • 

    • if the dimensions are larger, we calculate how much vias fit
      • 

    • 



\[
R_{via} = \frac{R_{coeff}}{n_x * n_y}   \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[\frac{mΩ}{\text{via count}}\right]
\]


\[
n_x = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{w - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


\[
n_y = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{h - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


    

  • Coefficient \(R_{coeff}\) is part of the tech files (Parasitic Tables)

      

    • defined for every via layer
      • 

    • in \(mΩ\) per via
      • 

    • Coefficient already includes the thickness aspect of the layer, so the formula works in 2D
      • 

    • 













6 KPEX/2.5D Engine


This analytical extraction engine is separate from the PEX25D interchange format described in Section 10.1. kpex extract --2.5D selects the engine; kpex pex25d generates a geometry and material description without running an engine.


Field solvers are precise, yet slow, they are useful to obtain a golden reference.


For most use cases, a faster engine is desirable. KPEX/MAGIC is such an engine, but the MAGIC code is tightly coupled with the database, layer/via design choices, and user interface of MAGIC. For example, it runs single-threaded.


Therefore, the KPEX 2.5D Engine intends to implement the concepts and formulas of MAGIC (see Section 5.2), but in a way that is best suited to the KLayout API, and is modular and open for parallel execution.







In Figure 9, we see that as in the KPEX/FasterCap engine (see Section 4), a “LVS” script is used to extract the connectivity information and create an LVS report database.


As mentioned in Section 1.4, KPEX uses the KLayout API. During the course of this project, in cooperation with Matthias Köfferlein, the KLayout API was extended, in order to simplify parasitic extraction.


The engine uses those new API classes to extract parasitic capacitances:


    

  • klayout.db.PolygonNeighborhoodVisitor (since 0.30.1): used during the extraction of overlap capacitances (see Section 5.5)
    • 

  • klayout.db.EdgeNeighborhoodVisitor (since 0.30.1): used during the extraction of sidewall capacitances (see Section 5.4) and fringe capacitances (see Section 5.6)
    • 

  • Geometry classes with properties in klayout.db (since 0.30.1): store net information directly on polygons, edges, edge pairs and boxes
    • 



The engine uses those new API classes to extract parasitic resistances:


    

  • klayout.pex module (since KLayout 0.30.2)

      

    • klayout.pex.RNetExtractor: used to extract resistance networks
      • 

    • klayout.pex.RExtractorTech: minimal process stack description for conductor and via layers
      • 

    • 





6.1 Choosing the Level of Detail


--mode CC keeps each connected net equipotential. --mode R breaks its conductors into a resistance network. --mode RC places extracted capacitances on that distributed network as well, so the position of a load along a wire affects the simulated response.


The capacitance model has separate area-overlap, facing-sidewall and fringe terms. Polygon integration preserves their geometric meaning for sloped boundaries (Section 6.2). It does not turn the analytical model into a field solver or remove the need to check its coefficients against the intended technology.


The halo limits which neighboring geometry participates in sidewall and fringe extraction. Keep the same halo and fringe normalization when comparing runs. Recent neighborhood batching and rectangular-shield interval subtraction reduce repeated geometric work while retaining the polygon path for general shapes. They do not justify shrinking the halo to obtain a faster result.






6.2 Capacitance of Sloped and Holed Polygons


A wire does not have to end in a rectangle. A taper, a diagonal segment, or a shield with a hole changes the distance to the neighboring conductor along the edge. KPEX/2.5D integrates that changing geometry using the same overlap, sidewall, and fringe models introduced in Section 5.2.


This extends where those models can be applied. It does not turn the analytical extraction into a three-dimensional field solution: the dielectric stack and fitted parasitic coefficients still determine the model’s accuracy.




6.2.1 Looking Along One Edge


For each source edge, imagine rotating the layout until that edge lies on the horizontal axis. Let \(x\) run along the edge and \(y\) point outwards from its conductor. The local coordinate system is attached to the edge, so a diagonal wire needs no special capacitance formula.


The neighborhood is divided into intervals where the facing boundaries remain straight. Within one interval:


    

  • A sidewall gap is a linear function \(d(x)\)
    • 

  • A fringe target has a near boundary \(n(x)\) and a far boundary \(f(x)\)
    • 

  • A shield can shorten either boundary or remove a part of the target
    • 
















A bounding box loses this information. It fills the empty space beside a triangle and across a hole. Using the minimum distance everywhere also assigns the closest part’s stronger coupling to the whole edge.


Overlap capacitance needs no distance integration in this plane. It is proportional to the actual unshielded intersection area, including the subtraction of holes:


\[
C_{\mathrm{overlap}} = \frac{k_{\mathrm{ov}}}{1000}\,A_{\mathrm{visible}}.
\]


Here \(k_{\mathrm{ov}}\) is in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}^2\), area is in \(\mu\mathrm{m}^2\), and the result is in \(\mathrm{fF}\).






6.2.2 Integrating a Changing Sidewall Gap


Take an edge interval of length \(L\) with endpoint gaps \(d_0\) and \(d_1\):


\[
d(x)=d_0+\frac{d_1-d_0}{L}\,x,\qquad 0\leq x\leq L.
\]


The technology fit adds an offset \(o\) to the physical gap. For a positive physical gap, a negative offset must not make the fitted separation zero or negative. KPEX/2.5D therefore uses


\[
s(d)=\max\left(d+o,\frac d2\right).
\]


The geometry factor is the integral of the reciprocal separation:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=\int_0^L \frac{dx}{s(d(x))}.
\]


For a full-pair sidewall coefficient \(k_{\mathrm{sw}}\) in \(\mathrm{aF}\), one directed edge contributes


\[
C_{\mathrm{sw,edge}}=\frac{k_{\mathrm{sw}}G_{\mathrm{sw}}}{2\cdot1000}
\quad [\mathrm{fF}].
\]


The two directed visits together count the pair once. The geometry integral introduces no additional half, and the conversion from \(\mathrm{aF}\) to \(\mathrm{fF}\) divides by \(1000\). This counting convention is separate from the shape of the gap (Section 5.4).


If the whole interval uses \(s=d+o\), the integral has a closed form:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=
\begin{cases}
\displaystyle \frac{L}{d_0+o}, & d_0=d_1,\\[8pt]
\displaystyle \frac{L}{d_1-d_0}
\ln\left(\frac{d_1+o}{d_0+o}\right), & d_0\ne d_1.
\end{cases}
\]


The logarithm is the result of integrating \(1/(a+bx)\). It is not a correction fitted specifically to diagonal wires. Reversing the edge exchanges \(d_0\) and \(d_1\) and changes both signs, leaving the result unchanged.


For a negative \(o\), the two separation branches meet at \(d=-2o\). If a taper crosses that gap, split its integral there. On the clamped part, integrate \(2/d\) instead of \(1/(d+o)\). The two branches agree at the split, so no capacitance jump is introduced.




6.2.2.1 Why the Mean Gap Is Insufficient


Consider \(L=4\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), a gap widening from \(0.2\) to \(0.6\,\mu\mathrm{m}\), and \(o=0.1\,\mu\mathrm{m}\). These values describe a geometry exercise, independently of any PDK coefficient:


\[
G_{\mathrm{sw}}=
\frac{4}{0.6-0.2}\ln\left(\frac{0.6+0.1}{0.2+0.1}\right)
=10\ln(7/3).
\]


Replacing the taper by its mean gap gives \(4/(0.4+0.1)=8\). The integral is larger because reducing a small gap strengthens coupling more than increasing an already large gap weakens it.


The first half of the edge carries the fraction


\[
\frac{C_{[0,L/2]}}{C_{[0,L]}}
=\frac{\ln(5/3)}{\ln(7/3)},
\]


which is greater than one half. This matters when the capacitance is assigned to different nodes of an extracted resistor network.








6.2.3 Integrating Fringe Across a Target


The fringe model uses a cumulative fraction


\[
F(y)=\frac{2}{\pi}\arctan\bigl(\alpha\max(0,y)\bigr).
\]


\(F(y)\) describes how much of the fringe is reached by distance \(y\). Its slope decreases with distance. A strip near the source edge therefore receives more fringe than an equally wide strip farther away.


For a strip extending from \(n(x)\) to \(f(x)\), the received fraction is \(F(f(x))-F(n(x))\). Integrating along the source edge gives


\[
C_{\mathrm{fringe}}=
\frac{k_{\mathrm{fr}}}{1000\,N}
\int_0^L \left[F(f(x))-F(n(x))\right]dx.
\]


\(k_{\mathrm{fr}}\) is the directional side-overlap coefficient in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}\). \(N\) describes halo normalization, explained below. The overlap table supplies the parameter \(\alpha\) for this source/target layer pair, while the side-overlap table supplies \(k_{\mathrm{fr}}\). They play different roles: one sets the distance dependence, the other its magnitude.


In the current coefficient convention, the numerical value of \(\alpha\) in \(\mu\mathrm{m}^{-1}\) is \(0.02\) times the overlap coefficient in \(\mathrm{aF}/\mu\mathrm{m}^2\). This scaling belongs to the empirical fringe model; it is not an identity between capacitance and inverse distance.















The near and far boundaries of a trapezoid are linear functions. Their integrals can be evaluated analytically using


\[
J(z)=z\arctan(z)-\frac12\ln(1+z^2),
\qquad J'(z)=\arctan(z).
\]


For \(q(x)=q_0+mx>0\), \(m\ne0\) and \(\alpha>0\):


\[
\int_a^b F(q(x))\,dx
=\frac{2}{\pi\alpha m}
\left[J(\alpha q(b))-J(\alpha q(a))\right].
\]


A constant boundary gives \((b-a)F(q_0)\). A boundary crossing zero is split there, because the part behind the source edge contributes no outward fringe. The implementation evaluates equivalent forms that avoid subtracting nearly equal numbers when the slope or \(\alpha\) is small.






6.2.4 Subtracting Shields and Keeping Holes


A nearer conductor on the same layer limits the lateral reach. Its sloping facing edge produces a sloping shadow, rather than a rectangle beginning at one mean distance. This shadow also applies when the nearby shape belongs to the same net or to the opposite side of the same polygon.


For a target on a different layer, conductors between the source and target provide additional shielding. The source-to-target ordering matters: a conductor beyond the target does not shield that target. Above and below the source are handled separately.


After subtracting these shields, a target may be concave or have holes. KPEX/2.5D partitions the remaining geometry into vertical trapezoids in the source edge’s local coordinates:


    

  1. Split at the distinct horizontal positions of polygon vertices
    2. 

  2. Find the boundary crossings within each strip
    3. 

  3. Pair successive crossings as filled intervals, leaving holes empty
    4. 

  4. Integrate each trapezoid and add its contribution
    5. 
















This is a partition of the visible polygon, not a replacement by rectangles. Intersections at a new strip boundary remain floating-point values for the capacitance calculation. Only the geometry drawn in the extraction report is rounded back onto the layout grid.


The small-contribution cutoff is applied to each resulting unshielded polygon before its internal trapezoids are emitted. A polygon that contributes more than \(0.0001\,\mathrm{fF}\) remains even if each trapezoid individually contributes less. A value equal to the cutoff is omitted. Changing the mathematical subdivision therefore does not change whether that polygon is retained.






6.2.5 Preserving the Profile When Geometry Is Cut


The total capacitance is not enough when a marker removes part of an edge or when RC extraction divides it between nodes. The taper example above has equal lengths on either side of its midpoint but unequal capacitances.


KPEX/2.5D retains an integral profile for a sloped contribution. A cut asks the profile for the capacitance over the retained interval. A later cut uses the original coordinates of that interval. It does not restart the distance ramp at its new left endpoint.


This makes three operations consistent:


    

  • Summing the parts reproduces the original contribution before cutoffs
    • 

  • An exclusion marker removes the capacitance carried by its covered geometry
    • 

  • RC node assignment uses the local capacitance density, rather than only the fraction of edge length
    • 



For overlap capacitance, the density within one layer pair is uniform per area, so area fractions remain appropriate.






6.2.6 Inspecting Sloped Wires


The sky130A pattern below has a tapered conductor A, a bent conductor B, and a rectangular conductor C. The A ↔︎ B gap varies along the taper, whereas part of the B ↔︎ C gap is constant.


GDS: sidewall_non_parallel_li1.gds.gz















From the klayout-pex source checkout, the committed LVS database allows the extraction to be repeated without running LVS:


lvsdb_dir=testdata/lvsdb/sky130A/test_patterns
kpex extract --pdk sky130A --mode CC --blackbox n \
  --lvsdb "$lvsdb_dir/sidewall_non_parallel_li1.lvsdb.gz" \
  --2.5D --halo 8 --scale y --report-caps y \
  --out-dir output_polygon_example


The example was checked with klayout-pex 0.9.0 and the KLayout Python module 0.30.13. --report-caps y adds each contribution and its geometry to the extraction report. Inspect the A ↔︎ B sidewall entries to see how the facing intervals follow the taper. The exported netlist combines the contributions belonging to the same pair of nets.






6.2.7 Halo, Grid and Model Limits


The halo is the finite lateral neighborhood searched around an edge. --halo overrides the technology’s side_halo, in \(\mu\mathrm{m}\). It changes which geometry is considered, so it is a modeling choice as well as a runtime limit.


The default --scale y normalizes the fringe fraction to that halo. For a positive overlap coefficient and halo \(h\), \(N=F(h)\), and a target occupying the full interval from \(0\) to \(h\) receives the full coefficient for that edge length. A zero overlap coefficient gives \(\alpha=0\) and zero fringe contribution before normalization. With --scale n, \(N=1\), so the tail beyond the halo remains omitted. A larger halo can change both the visible targets and, when scaling is enabled, the normalization of nearer ones.


The --scale flag here concerns fringe fractions. It is independent of SPICE .option scale, which controls the interpretation of selected device geometry parameters.


These limits matter when comparing results:


    

  • An overlap coefficient of exactly zero gives zero fringe, including with halo scaling enabled
    • 

  • Very small positive overlap coefficients approach a uniform distribution across a normalized halo
    • 

  • Rotating a layout onto an integer grid can move vertices and neighborhood boundaries slightly
    • 

  • Intervals no longer than one database unit are discarded to suppress degenerate edge neighborhoods
    • 

  • The analytical model does not resolve full three-dimensional corner fields or replace coefficient calibration
    • 



For a rotation comparison, keep the same physical dimensions, coefficient tables, halo, and scaling option. A finer database unit reduces geometric rounding. Quarter-turn rotations preserve integer-grid coordinates exactly; arbitrary angles usually do not.








6.3 Excluding Parts of the Layout


Some structures are better served by a model than by a 2.5D extraction: an inductor by an EM simulation, which also has its inductance, a hard block by a netlist of its own, or the power grid of a block by the extraction of the top level. FEM co-simulation for example matches measured mm-wave amplifiers better than an RC extraction (Sagouo Minko and Stander 2019). The rest of the layout should still be extracted, and connect to the model.


This raises four questions, which this section answers:


    

  • How does a layout say what the extraction should leave out, and for which layers?
    • 

  • What happens to the shapes there: can they just be removed, with dielectric in their place?
    • 

  • What about the capacitances between what is left out and what is not?
    • 

  • How does the rest of the layout connect to the model?
    • 



There are three ways to select what is left out, which follow the same rule (Section 6.3.3):







By default, nothing is left out, so that a netlist doesn’t change without one of these. Markers and cells are read from the GDS, so that these options need --gds, also together with --lvsdb, as an LVS database only has the shapes of nets.


The options work with --2.5D, --fastercap and --fastcap (Section 6.3.9), not with --magic.




6.3.1 What the PDKs Mark







The layer rules of the IHP PDKs don’t describe the markers beyond one line each. What the pair markers can mean follows from their names, as they name a pair of plates. Of the 533 GDS of the IHP reference layouts and LVS testcases, 25 have a marker, all of them noqrc of rfcmim.


By default, KPEX honors NoRCX.drawing and the pair markers. noqrc only takes effect on request, with --exclusion-marker-layer (Section 6.3.6): the extraction of the rfcmim already knows the device, in white-box mode it would lose the capacitor, and in a reference layout it would hit 2624 µm² of metal that isn’t part of the device.


sky130A and gf180mcuD have no layer for this, in their layer tables or in the cells and layouts looked at. SkyWater’s extraction rules leave parasitics to the models by device recognition (varactors, MIM capacitors, RF ESD diodes, precision poly resistors), and MAGIC by the property device of a cell, which zeroes the parasitics of the cell. So these PDKs take markers of the user (Section 6.3.6).






6.3.2 Why the Geometry Stays


Tools take one of three approaches, here by the public material of commercial tools:







Removing the shapes is the simple approach, but it changes what is outside them, as Figure 14 shows. A 2.5D extraction rests on the shielding by what is in between: neighbors reduce the coupling across a layer from 16.3 % to 1.8 % of the total, and it’s only negligible above a metal density threshold (Cong et al. 1997). The same holds for metal without a function: ignoring dummy fill gives errors above 30 %, and the fill on other layers matters more than the fill on the same layer (Kurokawa et al. 2004). Full-chip extractors handle grounded fill, floating fill needs a 3D solver (Kahng et al. 2006; Yu et al. 2006).







Table 11 has this for small layouts of ihp-sg13g2, in --mode CC, with FasterCap in brackets. FasterCap is no reference here, it only shows the same trend. “Coupling dropped” keeps the shape as a shield, but leaves out all of its capacitances, also those to the wires.







So the shapes stay: without them, the wires around them have wrong values, which neither the netlist nor the model can correct.












Note







With a marker over all layers, the parts of A and B within it are left out too, so the first rows of Table 11 apply to a neighbor like N, and to the parts near the edge of the marker. They apply fully where only some shapes are left out at a location: a marker of one layer (Section 6.3.6), a cell with routing over it (Section 6.3.7), or a net (Section 6.3.8).






The coil of a PDK inductor is an exception that does no harm: the deck of KPEX takes the metal within IND out of the conductors, so that it is no shield, but it is 30 µm from the edge of its polygon, beyond the halo of 8 µm, so that nothing outside the polygon is affected.






6.3.3 What Is Left Out


A conductor is in where it lies within what is left out on its layer, otherwise out. Each polygon of the merged markers, and each instance of a cut cell, stands for a model of its own, which is called a block below.







A capacitance partly within a marker is split: for an overlap by its area, for a sidewall or fringe along its edge. A fringe goes by the plate next to the edge, also on a well that goes on across a marker.


The resistance network has no resistance within a block. A via is within a block by its center, on both of its conductors, as vias can stick out past their metal, and the resistance of a part of a via would be made up. Otherwise it keeps its resistance and the metal it lands on.


Devices within a marker stay in the netlist, as the PDK inductors do. In white-box mode (--blackbox n), a capacitor within a marker is lost, as the device is removed and its plates are filtered. A warning names these devices. The devices of a cut cell are left out (Section 6.3.7).


A marker over routing costs that wire much of its capacitance, so a warning names the nets partly within markers, with their layers.






6.3.4 The Variants


Figure 15 shows the three values of --exclusion-markers for a wire through a marker. A --mode CC netlist has one node per net, so tie and ports are the same there, and a warning says that it has no ports for a model.









6.3.4.1 A Wire Through a Marker


Test pattern exclusion_wire_through, a Metal3 wire of 60 µm x 2 µm with a marker over its middle third, is the example of the variants below:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_wire_through.gds.gz
























6.3.4.2 ignore


What is within a marker is extracted like the rest of the layout. This is the default, as Figure 17 shows:


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 2.66364f
Cext_2 B sub! 2.66364f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.001
Rext_2 A B 2.596
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through



















6.3.4.3 tie


What is within a marker has no parasitics, and each net stays connected across it, so that the netlist simulates without a model. It’s useful to see what the rest of a layout adds, or if a model is only needed for some of the analyses (Figure 18):


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 0.951336f
Cext_2 A|B sub! 1.69065f
Cext_3 B sub! 0.951336f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.857956
Rext_2 A|B B 0.858
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through

















6.3.4.3.1 Metal Joined Only Outside the Marker


The metal within a marker stays apart where nothing within the marker joins it. In the test pattern exclusion_stubs (Figure 19), two stubs of a net end within the marker, which only the metal outside it joins. So their pins S1 and S2 stay two nodes, with 1.046 Ω to A each, as a tie would short the metal outside the marker.





















6.3.4.4 ports


Each cut of a net at a marker is a port of the netlist, for a model to connect (Figure 20):


.SUBCKT exclusion_wire_through A A_B__m0_0 A_B__m0_1 B sub!
Cext_1 A sub! 0.951336f
Cext_2 A_B__m0_0 sub! 0.845326f
Cext_3 A_B__m0_1 sub! 0.845326f
Cext_4 B sub! 0.951336f
Rext_1 A A|B 0.001
Rext_2 A A_B__m0_0 0.857956
Rext_3 A_B__m0_1 B 0.858
.ENDS exclusion_wire_through















A port is named after the pin of the net within the marker that is nearest to the cut, on its layer before others, otherwise <net>__m<marker>_<number>. So labels within a marker name the ports. In exclusion_stubs, these are S1 and S2. Such a pin only names a cut of the metal it is joined to within the marker, and not if the net has a pin of that label outside the marker, as a port is one node. A net entirely within a marker has a port at its pin.


--check accepts the pieces of a net that only these ports join. These pieces stay apart in the netlist, also where taps or wells would join them ideally otherwise, as that would short the model. And a part of a well beyond a cut keeps its port and its resistance, with the bulks of the devices on it. A bulk within the marker is a port of the model as well.


A port is one node, which is right across the current, also on a wide wire. Where the metal goes on beside a marker, along a cut, the whole cut would short that metal, so the port is a piece of 1 µm in the middle of the cut. The metal beside it then carries the current alone: test pattern cut_strip_along_wire, a wire of 100 µm x 1 µm with half of its width within a marker along 50 µm, has 8.78 Ω flat and 17.41 Ω with ports, as a port can’t connect a model in parallel to that metal.




6.3.4.4.1 Capacitances Between the Parts of a Net


Metal that only a model joins is one net in LVS, but apart in the netlist with ports, so the capacitances between it count, unlike within a net otherwise. In test pattern exclusion_hairpin (Figure 21), two Metal3 wires 2 µm apart end within the marker, where a bridge joins them. In exclusion_hairpin_open, the bridge has a gap, so they are two nets. With ports, both have the same values:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_hairpin.gds.gz




















With tie, the net stays connected, so these wires are a net like without a marker, which has no capacitances within it. In --mode CC, a net is one node, so there are no ports and no such capacitances.






6.3.4.4.2 Checking a Model


To check that a model fits, a test extracts the part of the wire within the marker on its own, as a stand-in for a model, connects it between the ports, and compares the port admittance in ngspice with the one of the flat extraction. They differ by 2.3 %, by the fringe of that part at the cuts, where the flat wire has no edges.










6.3.5 Examples




6.3.5.1 A Neighbor Outside a Marker


Test pattern exclusion_plate_neighbor (Figure 22), a Metal3 plate P just within a marker, with a Metal3 wire N 0.3 µm beside it. N keeps all of its values, as it is out, and P keeps only its capacitance to N.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_plate_neighbor.gds.gz




















Without a label on the plate, in exclusion_floating_plate_neighbor, nothing connects it to the netlist, so that the capacitance to it goes to the substrate: N ↔︎ VSUBS is 5.045 fF.






6.3.5.2 Two Markers


Two such plates P and Q, 0.5 µm apart. With a marker each (exclusion_plates_2_markers), they keep their 0.828 fF to each other, as neither model has it. With one marker over both (exclusion_plates_1_marker), the netlist has no capacitances at all.






6.3.5.3 Vias


Test pattern exclusion_via_stack, a wire from A to B on Metal2, with a bridge on Metal3 over a gap in the middle, with a marker around the bridge:







In exclusion_via_across, the center of the via is outside the marker, so it keeps its 2.031 Ω, and only the Metal3 within the marker has no resistance.






6.3.5.4 Devices


Test pattern exclusion_nmos_diode2 (Figure 23), with a marker over a MOS transistor. The metal of its nets leaves the marker on Metal1 and Metal2.


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_nmos_diode2.gds.gz















With tie, its terminals are on the nodes of the metal within the marker. With ports, each terminal is a port of its own, as the model connects them:


X$1 VSS__m0_2 VDD__m0_4 VDD__m0_5 sub! sg13_lv_nmos w=1.5e-07 l=1.7e-07


The bulk stays on the substrate, which is no conductor of the resistance network.








6.3.6 Markers of a Layer, of a Pair and of the User


--exclusion-marker-layer selects the markers, instead of those on by default. It takes the name of a marker of the PDK, or any GDS layer, for all layers of the stack (200/0) or for some (200/0:met2,met3). So a PDK without markers can have them too, such as sky130A and gf180mcuD, and --exclusion-markers ignore stays the default.


A marker of a layer leaves out only what is on that layer. In test pattern exclusion_plate_noqrc, a Metal3 plate P is between a Metal2 wire A and a Metal4 wire B, with Metal3.noqrc over the plate. So P loses its capacitance to the substrate, and the wires keep all of theirs, with the plate as a shield between them. This is the case that Table 11 is about.


A pair marker only leaves out the capacitances between its two layers, so it has no effect on the resistances. The same plate with m2m3 (exclusion_plate_pair_m2m3), and with m3sub (exclusion_plate_pair_m3sub):







The 0.198 fF that stay with m2m3 are the fringe to the part of A beyond the marker.






6.3.7 Cutting Out a Cell


--cut CELL[=PREFIX] leaves the instances of a cell to a model. CELL is a name or a glob pattern, and a cell within a cut cell is part of it. Each --cut needs instances of its own: the first one that matches a cell takes them.


What is left out:


    

  • The shapes of the cell, on the layers of the stack, so routing over it stays extracted, unlike with a marker over all layers:

      

    • metal and wells by their drawn layers, with the fill that LVS joins to them
      • 

    • what LVS computes from the diffusion (e.g. source and drain) by the diffusion of the cell
      • 

    • not its boundary or the overhang of its wells and implants, which take nothing of the layout under them
      • 

    • 

  • The devices of the cell, also for --check. As the netlist of LVS is flat, they go by what the cell draws at their terminals, on the layers that LVS makes a device of that class from, which the tech info has (the diffusion and the gate of a MOS, the marker of a resistor, a diode, a BJT or a capacitor):

      

    • on each layer, the cell has to draw a polygon at all terminals, and more of them than the rest of the layout, as a diffusion can go on beyond a cell, and a tap can overlap the one of a neighbor
      • 

    • so a device stays if it’s under the boundary or the fill of a cell, beside it on the same diffusion, or has only wires of the cell on its terminals
      • 

    • and fill, a boundary or a wire of the top cell leaves a device to the cell
      • 

    • 

  • Diffusion that no layer draws, which LVS fills up for a device of the cell (e.g. the drain of an LDMOS, across the gap to its gate), but not what the rest of the layout draws
    • 



--cut-keep-net NET takes the shapes of a net out of the cell, also its wells, so that they are extracted like the rest of the layout, e.g. a guard ring.


Where a net enters the cell is a port of the netlist, as with --exclusion-markers ports, named:


    

  • <prefix>__<label>, by the labels of the cell on the metal it is joined to within the cell, nearest first. Several cuts of that metal share the port, as they are one pin of the model
    • 

  • <prefix>__<terminal>, for a terminal of a device of the cell on the metal around it, numbered if the block has several such nodes on a net (X__S_0, X__S_1)
    • 

  • <prefix>__<net>_<number> otherwise
    • 



The prefix:


    

  • is PREFIX for a single instance, with a number for several (x_0, x_1)
    • 

  • is by default the name of the cell with a number per cell (coil_0)
    • 

  • has letters, digits and _ only, as it names ports
    • 

  • has to differ for each instance, so --cut a=S_0 --cut b=S is an error if b has several instances
    • 



Test pattern cut_block_with_mos has the MOS of the design nmos_diode2 in the cell block, whose pins VDD and VSS on Metal3 the top cell wires on to A and B, and a Metal5 wire R over the cell (Figure 24). With --cut block=X:


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cut_block_with_mos.gds.gz







.SUBCKT cut_block_with_mos A X__VSS B X__VDD sub! R
Cext_1 A B 0.397445f
Cext_2 A R 0.016564f
Cext_3 A sub! 0.197343f
Cext_4 A X__VDD 0.07352f
Cext_5 B R 0.0584666f
Cext_6 B sub! 0.221065f
Cext_7 R sub! 1.40824f
Cext_8 R X__VDD 0.194269f
Cext_9 R X__VSS 0.0809391f
Cext_10 sub! X__VDD 0.178802f
Cext_11 sub! X__VSS 0.178581f
Cext_12 X__VDD X__VSS 0.4502f
Rext_1 A X__VSS 2.86
Rext_2 B X__VDD 2.86
.ENDS cut_block_with_mos


There is no MOS, the two nets end on the ports for the model, the wire R keeps its capacitances, also to the metal of the cell, and the 2.86 Ω are the ones of the wires of the top cell.






6.3.8 Leaving Out a Net


--exclude-net NET, a name or a glob pattern, is for a net that something else models or drives, such as the power grid of a block:


    

  • it has no resistance, so the netlist has one node for it, which also all of its device terminals are on
    • 

  • it has no capacitance to the substrate
    • 

  • the capacitances between it and other nets stay, as they are the load of those nets, also between two excluded nets, and to a well of another net
    • 



exclusion_plate_neighbor with --exclude-net P gives the values of tie in Table 15, without needing a marker or a GDS. exclusion_nmos_diode2 with --exclude-net 'V*' in --mode RC has no resistor at all, and only 0.492 fF between VDD and VSS.


The values of the nets around it are as without the option, as the net stays in the field model. Unlike with a block, this goes by the name of the net, so that a large grid doesn’t slow down the extraction.






6.3.9 Field Solvers


A field solver only tells the capacitances between its conductors, not where they end on them. So with these options, a net is one conductor for its part outside the blocks, and one for each set of blocks it is within, as these can overlap. The substrate is a conductor of its own, also if its net has metal. There are no panels between the conductors of a net, as those would be coincident. The matrix goes through the rule of Table 12, and the parts of each net are summed up: with all at the same potential, the charges they induce add up to the charge of the net as one conductor.


The netlist of a field solver has one node per net, so it has no ports, as with --mode CC. A warning says so, with ports and with --cut. It also has no capacitances between the parts of a net that only a model joins.


FasterCap gives the same picture as Table 15 and Table 21, with its own values:







Where a net is two conductors, the values around it differ by up to 2.5 %, as the mesh differs at the ends of the parts.






6.3.10 Use Cases




6.3.10.1 Inductor of the PDK, with EM Model


The pcells draw NoRCX.drawing, and the LVS deck of KPEX recognizes the inductor as a subcircuit with its terminals at its leads, so a model replaces it by its name, without any ports. What --exclusion-markers changes is the rest of what is within its polygon, such as a wire under the coil (exclusion_inductor2_wire_under, Figure 25, with --blackbox y):


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/exclusion_inductor2_wire_under.gds.gz




















So a model of the coil that has that wire in its simulation should be used with tie or ports, and one without with ignore.


This is what #121 asks for: most of a circuit with the 2.5D engine, and EM models for the sensitive RF parts.






6.3.10.2 Coil of LC Oscillator


#213 extracts the core of an oscillator without the coil of its tank, which has an EM-fitted model, but with its leads and its guard ring, with ports where the core meets the coil. Outside KPEX, this took a cut of the GDS, with workarounds for the recognition texts of devices and the labels of child cells.


Test pattern cut_coil (Figure 26) is a small layout with these parts, not that design:


    

  • the cell coil, with a TopMetal2 loop with stubs of its leads, a center tap on TopMetal1, and a TopMetal1 guard ring around them, and the labels LA, LB and CT
    • 

  • wires of the top cell, which go on from the stubs to OSCP, OSCN and VCT, and a stub with the label VDD on the guard ring
    • 

  • a Metal5 wire VC of the top cell under the coil
    • 



GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cut_coil.gds.gz















With kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --gds cut_coil.gds.gz --2.5D --mode RC --cut coil=xind --cut-keep-net VDD:


.SUBCKT cut_coil OSCN OSCP VCT xind__CT xind__LA xind__LB VC VDD sub!
Cext_1 OSCN sub! 1.04552f
Cext_2 OSCP sub! 1.04552f
Cext_3 VC VDD 2.1086f
Cext_4 VC sub! 8.43019f
Cext_5 VC xind__CT 0.89613f
Cext_6 VC xind__LA 0.398954f
Cext_7 VC xind__LB 0.398954f
Cext_8 VCT sub! 1.17194f
Cext_9 VDD sub! 30.0624f
Cext_10 VDD xind__LA 0.110313f
Cext_11 VDD xind__LB 0.110313f
Cext_12 sub! xind__CT 0.925084f
Cext_13 sub! xind__LA 0.703486f
Cext_14 sub! xind__LB 0.703486f
Rext_1 OSCN OSCN|OSCP|VCT 0.001
Rext_2 OSCN xind__LB 0.0348333333333
Rext_3 OSCP xind__LA 0.0348333333333
Rext_4 VCT xind__CT 0.0855
.ENDS cut_coil


The model goes between the ports, in the netlist that includes this one:


XCORE OSCN OSCP VCT xind__CT xind__LA xind__LB VC VDD 0 cut_coil
XL xind__LA xind__LB xind__CT coil_em_model


--mode CC shows what is left out, with the net of the coil being OSCN,OSCP,VCT:







The wire VC, which is no shape of the cell, keeps all of its capacitances, also to the coil, which a model wouldn’t know. Without --cut-keep-net VDD, the guard ring is left to the model too, and the net VDD enters the cell at the port xind__VDD_0.


To check that this fits, a test extracts the coil on its own (cut_coil_model), as a stand-in for a model, connects it between the ports, and compares the port admittance in ngspice with the one of the flat extraction:


    

  • the resistances, between OSCP, OSCN and VCT, are the same within 0.1 %
    • 

  • so are the values of VC and VDD to each other and to the substrate, and their capacitances to the coil in sum, which are at the ports instead of along the coil
    • 

  • the coil to the substrate is 10 % higher, as a model on its own has no shielding by the wires around it
    • 



Compared with the cut of the GDS:


    

  • running LVS on the whole layout keeps the recognition texts of the devices, and needs no selection of the labels of child cells
    • 

  • the ports go by the metal, wherever a net enters, so that the leads need no pins, and the nets their names from the top level
    • 

  • what a block has around it stays in the field model
    • 



--exclusion-markers ports does the same without a cell, for a marker drawn over the coil, inside the guard ring, as in test pattern exclusion_coil_guard_ring (Figure 27), whose labels name the ports. As a marker applies to all layers, routing through it is left out too.




















The second part of #213, every label a port for the wiring between hard blocks, is what the netlists of --mode R and RC do for the labels of a net in the top cell. Labels in the cells of the blocks become ports with --cut.






6.3.10.3 Power Grid of Block


#85 extracts a block whose power grid is part of the top level:


kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --gds block.gds.gz --2.5D --mode RC \
             --exclude-net VDD --exclude-net VSS


So VDD and VSS are ideal nodes of the netlist, with all device terminals on them, and each signal keeps its load to them, as the grid stays in the field model. For debugging, leaving out the resistance of one net at a time shows what it adds to a simulation.








6.3.11 Limits


    

  • A model whose simulation includes a neighbor counts their coupling twice, unless the neighbor is within the block too. The boundary of such hybrid flows seems to be little studied: the literature has the error of ports within an EM model (Rautio 2008), but no work on the double counting was found
    • 

  • A model extracted or simulated on its own has no shielding by what is around it (Section 6.3.10)
    •
