  • The coupling of a conductor outside to one within a block lands on the nearest node of its net, which is approximate in a large block
    • 

  • KLayout’s square counting, which the resistance network uses, has the current along the longest edge of each convex part of a polygon, also without these options. So a part beyond a cut that is shorter than it is wide has too little resistance, which matters on wells: two nwell taps of r_ntap_pair_nwell_li1_m1, with a marker of 2 µm between them across the nwell of 7 µm, have 212 Ω with tie, 1948 Ω by tessellation. Wires at an angle have too little too, a Metal3 wire of 60 µm x 1 µm has 5.28 Ω at 0° and 2.65 Ω at 45°, and a corner of a marker on such a wire can give several times the value of the whole wire
    • 

  • A net that goes on from one cut cell to another, where they abut, has no port between them, for which a warning names the net and the cells
    • 

  • --cut of an instance at an angle other than a multiple of 90°, or of one with such an instance below it, is an error, as the LVS database only has the bounding boxes of the shapes of such an instance
    • 

  • There is no comparison with silicon or an EM simulation yet: the reference of tie, ports and --cut is the flat extraction
    • 

  • The exports of 2.5D scenes for other field solvers don’t honor these options. MAGIC doesn’t either, so they are an error together with it
    • 









6.4 Connecting the Extracted Netlist


A parasitic netlist has two jobs: describe the layout’s electrical network, and expose an interface that the testbench can call correctly. A correct capacitance attached to the wrong positional pin is still a wrong simulation.


--schematic supplies two pieces of that interface to KPEX/2.5D: the order of the top-level ports, and names for devices that can be matched unambiguously. It does not replace a full LVS comparison. The checks in Section 7 answer narrower questions about missing devices, geometry totals, pins and connectivity.




6.4.1 Choosing Which Labels Become Ports


A label inside a child cell often names an internal net. Making every such label a top-level port can expose implementation details of a block to its testbench. Conversely, a layout without top-level pin labels may rely on the labels of its children.







auto is the default. --port-labels top needs --gds, including when an LVS database supplies the extracted nets. Substrate handling and top-level text-only ports remain in place. Selecting top-level labels does not remove the child geometry or the internal nets from extraction.






6.4.2 Keeping Positional Calls Correct


SPICE connects a subcircuit call by position. The first node in the call connects to the first port of its .subckt declaration, regardless of the spelling of the two names.


KPEX/2.5D defines the exported order as follows:


    

  • With --schematic, the matching top subcircuit’s ports come first, in schematic order
    • 

  • Any remaining ports follow, sorted by name, comparing without case first and exact spelling second
    • 

  • Without a usable schematic top, all exported ports use that name order
    • 

  • Matching ignores case, while the exported spelling comes from the extracted net
    • 



This applies to CC, R and RC, to reduced netlists, to SPICE and VACASK, and to the port lists recorded in kpex_result.json. It changes the interface order, not which physical net each port connects to. In CC, several labels on one equipotential net can remain one exported port; its earliest schematic alias determines its position.




6.4.2.1 Transistor with Schematic Port Order


Download ordered.spice, whose top declaration is .subckt nfet_li1 S G D and whose transistor is named Xtail. From the KPEX source directory, run:


kpex extract --pdk sky130A --2.5D --mode CC --blackbox y \
  --gds testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz \
  --schematic ordered.spice --out-netlist ordered-extracted.spice


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/nfet_li1.gds.gz


The declaration and device lines from that run are:


.SUBCKT nfet_li1 S G D sky130_gnd
Xtail D G S sky130_gnd sky130_fd_pr__nfet_01v8 l=0.15 w=0.65 as=0.169 ad=0.169
+ ps=1.82 pd=1.82















The top-level interface starts with S G D. The substrate sky130_gnd, absent from the schematic’s port declaration, follows them. The transistor line has its own model terminal order; it need not have the same order as the top-level interface. For this symmetric MOS device, exchanging source and drain still permits the match.








6.4.3 Following Schematic Device Names


Device naming needs a schematic .subckt whose name matches the layout top cell. Port ordering can additionally use the sole uncalled subcircuit when the top name differs; that fallback does not rename devices.


Matching uses the device mappings of the technology, connectivity and device geometry. A successful match retains the schematic name, as Xtail above. Devices inside schematic subcircuits can retain hierarchical paths such as X1.Xtail. Parallel layout fingers of one schematic MOS receive suffixes such as _0, _1 and _2.


Names alone are not evidence that two devices correspond. Indistinguishable parallel schematic instances, missing model mappings or an ambiguous comparison keep layout-derived names and produce a warning. An assignment that would create duplicate output names is rejected. The model mapping still selects the proper SPICE designator, so a native schematic M may be emitted through an X wrapper when that is the PDK’s model interface.






6.4.4 Keeping Geometry Units Separate from Electrical Values


The SPICE directives .option scale=1u and .options scale=1u set one geometry scale for the whole parsed netlist. They are not per-device or per-model settings. A declaration inside a subcircuit still supplies that same global setting.


For scale \(s\), the schematic geometry evaluator applies:







An X parameter named w is not automatically a length: its meaning belongs to the wrapper. If the wrapper is defined in the input, its native devices receive scaling after parameter evaluation. For an external model wrapper, the technology’s device mapping translates its declared units into the layout units used for matching and checks.


This distinction avoids scaling twice. The technology mapping describes the model interface; .options scale describes the netlist’s global geometry convention. Neither should be inferred from the other. Diode area factors and other model-specific parameters also cannot be treated as physical areas just because of their names.


The schematic reader accepts only scale on .option or .options. Keep simulator analyses, .model, .include, .lib and unrelated options in the testbench or model library, outside this input. It is a circuit description reader, not a complete simulation-deck reader.


The parser accepts a finite positive SPICE number, including suffixes. 1u and 1000n express the same scale. SPICE suffixes are case-insensitive: M means milli, and MEG means mega. Identical repeated declarations are accepted, while conflicting values, zero and negative scales are rejected.


The extraction argument --scale y is a different setting: it normalizes the fringe model at the halo boundary (Section 6.2). It does not rescale layout coordinates or SPICE device geometry.






6.4.5 Including Both Files in a VACASK Testbench


Conversion preserves the global setting in a companion options fragment. Download geometry-scale.spice, which contains a native Mnative and an external Xwrapped in parallel, both with w=4 l=2, under .option scale=1u:


netlist convert geometry-scale.spice --to vacask \
  --out-netlist geometry-scale.inc


The circuit include contains:


subckt pair (d g s b)
  Mnative (d g s b) nmos w=4 l=2 ad=3 as=5 pd=7 ps=11
  Xwrapped (d g s b) external w=4 l=2 ad=3 as=5 pd=7 ps=11
ends















The companion geometry-scale.options.inc contains:


options scale=1e-06


Include the circuit at circuit scope, and the options inside the testbench’s existing control block, before analyses:


Geometry scale example

include "geometry-scale-models.inc"
include "geometry-scale.inc"
xpair (d g 0 0) pair
model supply vsource
vd (d 0) supply dc=1 mag=1
vg (g 0) supply dc=1

control
  include "geometry-scale.options.inc"
  analysis op1 op
  analysis ac1 ac values=[1e6]
endc


Save the complete testbench beside the converted files and run vacask geometry-scale.sim. Its operating-point and AC analyses both run with the fragment above.


The example model file defines external as a wrapper around the same native model. The native device therefore sees a width of 4 µm and length of 2 µm in both paths. The X arguments remain unchanged so that the wrapper passes them on in its expected units.


The options affect the whole simulation, including other included circuits and external wrappers. Combining circuits that assume different global scales requires normalizing their model interfaces first. Omitting the options file or applying a second scale to the instance values changes the geometry.


kpex extract --netlist-format vacask --out-netlist extracted.inc also writes a companion extracted.options.inc. Keep both files together, even when the options set scale=1. A converter does not translate model libraries: the testbench must supply compatible VACASK models. With PDK wrappers, pass --pdk to netlist convert so that multiplier handling follows their declared interfaces.


The examples were verified with klayout-pex 0.9.0 and KLayout 0.30.13. The port-order and naming guarantees are independent of the capacitance coefficients that may change in subsequent releases.










7 Checking Extracted Netlists


A plausible simulation result does not establish that an extracted netlist is complete. A device terminal can be disconnected from the resistance of its wire, a port can be missing, or a reduction can remove the loss that matters at the operating frequency. These failures need different comparisons.


KPEX/2.5D checks the following stages:







The structural checks guard the translation from layout connectivity into a netlist. The admittance check guards a subsequent approximation. The device comparison examines the physical capacitance estimate itself. Passing one does not imply that the other two pass.




7.1 Preserving Layout Connectivity


Resistance extraction splits one layout net into many nodes. These node names need not resemble the original net name, and device names may come from the schematic (Section 6.4.3). The structural comparison therefore follows the layout’s net identities and device identities, rather than trying to infer connectivity from spelling.


For each original net, KPEX follows the connected component formed by its parasitic resistors. Capacitors do not join these components: they couple nets electrically, but do not make a DC connection.


The comparison looks for:


    

  • Original nets missing from the expanded netlist
    • 

  • Resistors that incorrectly join two original nets
    • 

  • Resistor components that reach no original net or model interface port
    • 

  • Device terminals attached to the wrong net’s resistor network
    • 

  • Device terminals attached to a different node than their extracted terminal port
    • 

  • Missing device instances, or retained whiteboxed devices that would count their capacitance twice
    • 

  • Missing ports and ports that touch nothing, with the exceptions required by exclusion interfaces
    • 

  • Node names that collide when SPICE treats names without regard to case
    • 



For capacitance, the comparison first maps the distributed nodes back to their original nets. It then sums the parasitic capacitors for every pair of nets, and compares these sums with the extraction summary. The relative tolerance is \(10^{-9}\); this comparison allows rounding, not a physical modeling error. A capacitance to the substrate is omitted from this comparison if the chosen substrate connection shorts its two endpoints together.




7.1.1 Choosing Whether a Structural Problem Stops the Run


In --mode RC, structural problems fail the run by default. In the other modes they are warnings by default. --check y makes them failures explicitly, and --check n accepts the netlist while keeping the warnings visible.


The checks run on the full extracted network before reduction. A reduction therefore cannot hide a structural defect by removing the affected nodes. For a structural failure found after extraction, the netlist remains available for inspection.


A separate warning identifies nets with parasitic elements but no device terminal or port that can drive them. Floating fill can legitimately produce this warning. A supply rail under a wrong label can produce it too, so it deserves review. This warning alone does not fail --check.








7.2 Comparing with the Schematic


With --schematic, KPEX also compares the extracted devices with the schematic, using the technology’s device mappings (Section 3.6). These checks supplement LVS; they do not perform a complete schematic-versus-layout topology comparison.




7.2.1 Comparing Device Quantities


Counting instances is insufficient. One schematic MOS instance can become several parallel fingers in the layout. Conversely, a layout extractor can combine devices. The comparison uses totals that survive these representations:


    

  • Device-class presence
    • 

  • Total \(W L\) when both dimensions are mapped, or total area when an area is mapped instead
    • 

  • Total \(W\) for mapped MOS devices
    • 

  • Total mapped multiplicity, such as emitter count
    • 



Multipliers and the number of hierarchical instances are included. Schematic dimensions are converted back to the LVS units before summation, including the SPICE geometry scaling discussed in Section 6.4.4. The relative tolerance for device totals is \(10^{-6}\).


A missing parameter is not silently replaced by an invented value. If the schematic leaves a relevant quantity to a model default, the corresponding total is left out and reported. A class without mapped totals is checked for presence only. Equal totals can still conceal an incorrectly wired device, which is why they do not replace LVS.






7.2.2 Comparing Pins and Ports


The top schematic subcircuit is selected by the layout cell name, without regard to case. If that name is absent, the schematic must have exactly one subcircuit that no other element calls.


The comparison reports schematic pins without extracted ports, and extracted ports without schematic pins. It accounts for interfaces that extraction adds or treats specially:


    

  • The selected substrate net may be global in the schematic
    • 

  • Exclusion-marker and cut-cell model ports are extra interfaces
    • 

  • A schematic pin that reaches only mapped bulk terminals can be absent from the extracted ports
    • 

  • A bulk-only pin is compared normally if an extracted port has its name
    • 



Port order is a separate interface contract, described in Section 6.4.2.








7.3 Checking the Response after Reduction


A smaller netlist should present nearly the same electrical response to its surroundings. Rather than comparing resistor counts or individual component values, the admittance check asks:




For the same terminal voltages at this frequency, how much do the resulting terminal currents change?




The check is optional because exact elimination can be more expensive than the reduction itself. It works with netlist reduce, and with kpex extract --2.5D --reduce floating or --reduce ticer in R or RC mode.




7.3.1 From Branches to Terminal Admittance


At frequency \(f\), a branch with conductance \(g\) and capacitance \(c\) has complex admittance


\[
y(f)=g+j\omega c, \qquad \omega=2\pi f.
\]


A branch between nodes \(a\) and \(b\) adds \(+y\) to both diagonal entries of the nodal admittance matrix, and \(-y\) to the two off-diagonal entries. This gives


\[
\mathbf i = \mathbf Y(f)\,\mathbf v,
\qquad \mathbf Y(f)=\mathbf G+j\omega\mathbf C.
\]


Partition the nodes into terminals \(t\) that the surrounding circuit can observe, and internal nodes \(i\) that it cannot drive directly:


\[
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf i_t\\\mathbf 0\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf Y_{tt}&\mathbf Y_{ti}\\
\mathbf Y_{it}&\mathbf Y_{ii}
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}\mathbf v_t\\\mathbf v_i\end{bmatrix}.
\]


Eliminating the internal voltages gives the terminal response


\[
\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{term}}
=\mathbf Y_{tt}-\mathbf Y_{ti}\mathbf Y_{ii}^{-1}\mathbf Y_{it}.
\]


This is a Schur complement. The implementation performs sparse, complex node elimination rather than forming a dense inverse. For one internal star node, eliminating it adds a branch between each pair of its neighbors:


\[
y_{ab}^{\mathrm{added}}=
\frac{y_{an}y_{nb}}{\sum_k y_{nk}}.
\]


This evaluation uses the full complex admittances at the requested frequency. It is independent of the approximate low-frequency reduction described in Section 9.


The terminals include the subcircuit ports, global and ground nodes, nodes touched by non-plain-R/C lines, and nodes selected with netlist reduce --keep. In particular, device and subcircuit terminals remain observable. The global reference 0 is also included so that added tie resistors affect the comparison.


Each subcircuit and the top level are evaluated separately. Components with no path to an observed terminal at that frequency do not contribute. At DC, capacitors are open circuits. The check does not add artificial ground conductances to make an isolated component solvable.






7.3.2 Comparing the Two Matrices


The reported error is


\[
\varepsilon(f)=
\frac{\left\|\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{reduced}}(f)
                 -\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{original}}(f)\right\|_F}
     {\left\|\mathbf Y_{\mathrm{original}}(f)\right\|_F},
\qquad
\|\mathbf Y\|_F=\sqrt{\sum_{a,b}|Y_{ab}|^2}.
\]


Both real and imaginary parts contribute. The check reads the written netlists, so its result includes rounded component values and any real tie resistors introduced by reduction.


The default limit is --check-max-relative-error 0.01, or 1%. Equality with the limit passes. The limit must be strictly between zero and one.


There is no absolute-error floor. A tiny capacitance is still compared relatively. Two zero matrices have zero error, while a nonzero reduced response against a zero original response has infinite error.






7.3.3 Choosing Frequencies


Use a single frequency when one operating point is the question. Use a range when the circuit must behave across a band:


netlist reduce extracted.spice \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 10G \
  --check-points-per-decade 10 \
  --check-include-dc


--check-frequency-range takes two arguments, the start and stop frequencies. SPICE suffixes are accepted. The endpoints are included, and the samples are logarithmically spaced. The default density is ten points per decade. A partial final decade still includes the exact upper endpoint.


The range requires \(0<f_{\mathrm{start}}\le f_{\mathrm{stop}}\). Equal endpoints produce one positive-frequency sample. --check-include-dc adds a separate sample at zero. For a DC-only check, use --check-frequency 0 instead.


Every sample in every checked scope must pass. The report names the worst sampled error and its frequency. A passing sweep covers those samples, not every frequency between them. Increase the density near an important transition or inspect a simulator response when that distinction matters.






7.3.4 Example: Losing the Series Resistance of a Capacitor


Download the original series-rc.spice. The internal node n has a time constant \(\tau=RC=100\,\mathrm{ps}\). Choosing a threshold of 1n allows its elimination:


netlist reduce series-rc.spice --ticer-tau 1n \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 1G \
  --check-points-per-decade 2 --check-include-dc \
  --out-netlist series-rc-reduced.spice


The input contains:


.SUBCKT series_rc A B
R1 A n 100
C1 n B 1p
.ENDS series_rc


The written reduced netlist contains:


.SUBCKT series_rc A B
Cred_1 A B 1p
.ENDS series_rc







For this circuit the original and reduced branch admittances are


\[
y_{\mathrm{original}}=\frac{j\omega C}{1+j\omega RC},
\qquad y_{\mathrm{reduced}}=j\omega C.
\]


Their two-terminal matrices have the same sign pattern, so the Frobenius error reduces to the scalar relative error:


\[
\varepsilon(f)=
\frac{|y_{\mathrm{reduced}}-y_{\mathrm{original}}|}
     {|y_{\mathrm{original}}|}
=\omega RC \quad (f>0).
\]


The run checks eight points, including DC, and exits with code 1. Its reported worst relative Frobenius error is 0.628319 at 1G Hz, against the 0.01 limit. At 1Meg Hz alone it would pass, with relative error 0.000628319.















A smaller threshold preserves the internal node in this example:


netlist reduce series-rc.spice --ticer-tau 1p \
  --check-frequency-range 1Meg 1G \
  --check-points-per-decade 2 --check-include-dc \
  --out-netlist series-rc-kept.spice


This run exits with code 0 and reports zero error at every sampled frequency. It keeps one resistor, one capacitor and three nodes. In a larger network, reducing the threshold usually trades fewer eliminated nodes for a closer response.






7.3.5 Limits of the Admittance Check


The matrix comparison covers the plain, numerically valued resistors and capacitors that the reduction reads. It does not simulate nonlinear device models, resolve a transistor’s bias point, or establish that the extracted parasitic values match silicon.


A relative norm over the whole matrix is not a separate relative bound on every small matrix entry. Nor does a small admittance error guarantee an acceptable quality factor: a small dissipative part can matter even when the much larger capacitive response dominates the norm. Keep the full network or use a sufficiently small reduction threshold when loss is important, and inspect the relevant circuit response.


Exact elimination can create many new couplings. The check limits each evaluation to 100,000 nodes/coupling entries and 1,000,000 coupling updates. It also limits the complete request to 1,001 frequency points and 10,000,000 graph entries/coupling updates across all scopes and samples. Exceeding a limit, or encountering an unevaluable numerical result, fails the requested check rather than silently accepting an unchecked network.








7.4 Comparing Device Capacitance with a Model


A blackboxed capacitor keeps its device model in the netlist. KPEX suppresses coupling between its internal plates so that the netlist does not count that capacitance twice. Ordinarily, that suppression also hides a useful diagnostic: how closely would the geometry-based extraction agree with the device’s nominal capacitance?


--check-device-caps observes those otherwise suppressed contributions. It does not add them to the exported netlist. The prerequisites are --gds, --2.5D, --blackbox y, and --mode CC or --mode RC.




7.4.1 Selecting the Geometry


The comparison identifies the selected device’s recognition marker in the original layout, using its terminal geometry and the recognition layers declared by the technology. It then observes coupling only when both participating plate shapes:


    

  • Belong to that same marker
    • 

  • Belong to the selected pair of terminal nets
    • 

  • Lie wholly inside the marker
    • 



The plate polygons are tagged, rather than clipped. Clipping at the marker boundary would manufacture new edges and therefore change sidewall and fringe contributions. A plate crossing that boundary is reported as unevaluable instead.


The comparison accumulates overlap, sidewall and fringe contributions separately:


\[
C_{\mathrm{geometry}}=
C_{\mathrm{overlap}}+C_{\mathrm{sidewall}}+C_{\mathrm{fringe}},
\qquad
r=\frac{C_{\mathrm{geometry}}}{C_{\mathrm{reference}}}.
\]


This is a device-local measurement. Substrate capacitance, coupling to external routing, and other capacitors connected between the same two net names are not a substitute for it. Output exclusions do not turn it into a subtraction of two whole-net capacitance totals.


Ambiguous geometry is not guessed. Missing or overlapping recognition markers, a marker containing another device’s terminals, shorted selected terminals, and missing internal plate geometry are reported as errors or unevaluable comparisons.






7.4.2 Using the Technology’s Nominal Reference


With no filename after --check-device-caps, the reference comes from the technology’s device mapping (Section 3.6.1). The mapping supplies an expression, its valid parameter domain, a source and its nominal assumptions. It is evaluated using the mapped device parameters.


KPEX does not search simulator model libraries at runtime or use an arbitrary LVS capacitance placeholder as the reference. Unsupported metal capacitors are listed as unchecked. If the layout has no available references, the requested comparison fails with an explanation.


There are no default ratio bounds. An evaluable automatic comparison is informational, not a declaration that the extraction is accurate enough for a circuit. This matters especially when the nominal model is itself an engineering estimate.






7.4.3 Example: MOM Plates below a Separate Route


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/v0.9.0/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns/cap_cmomf_w10u_l25u_m2_m4_m5_wire.gds.gz















The ihp-sg13g2 example has a cap_cmomf device with Metal2–Metal4 plates, width \(10\,\mu\mathrm m\) and length \(25\,\mu\mathrm m\). A separate Metal5 route on net X crosses above it. The model reference is the nominal mutual capacitance of mim_top ↔︎ mim_btm, with no corner or mismatch variation.


Set KPEX_DIR to the source checkout. This command uses its committed LVS database as well as the GDS, so that the comparison can find the original recognition marker. Here --scale y normalizes the fringe response at the halo, independently of SPICE geometry scaling:


pattern=cap_cmomf_w10u_l25u_m2_m4_m5_wire
layouts="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/designs/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
lvsdbs="$KPEX_DIR/testdata/lvsdb/ihp-sg13g2/test_patterns"
kpex extract --pdk ihp-sg13g2 --2.5D --mode CC \
  --blackbox y --halo 8 --scale y \
  --gds "$layouts/$pattern.gds.gz" \
  --lvsdb "$lvsdbs/$pattern.lvsdb.gz" \
  --check-device-caps --out-dir checks-mom \
  --out-result checks-mom.json


With klayout-pex 0.9.0, including the sidewall counting correction and refreshed nominal coefficients, the comparison reports:


$1 (cap_cmomf), mim_top / mim_btm:
marker coupling 236.403 fF, model reference 228.75 fF,
ratio 1.03345 (informational)


The device comparison is kept separately from the parasitic netlist. The netlist retains the compact-model instance and the external couplings, including those to X and the substrate. checks-mom.json records the comparison in device_capacitance_checks, including the three contributions in farads, the ratio, the reference source and its assumptions.






7.4.4 Supplying References and Acceptance Bounds


An explicit JSON file replaces the automatic selection. It can select one device and terminal pair, supply an independent reference, and optionally make the comparison a pass/fail check. For the preceding example, this reference file specifies an illustrative ±5% acceptance interval:


{
  "format_version": 1,
  "references": [
    {
      "device": "$1",
      "device_class": "cap_cmomf",
      "terminals": ["mim_top", "mim_btm"],
      "capacitance": "228.75f",
      "min_ratio": 0.95,
      "max_ratio": 1.05
    }
  ]
}


Repeat the example command with --check-device-caps mom-reference.json. These bounds pass for the recorded ratio 1.03345, producing exit code 0.




7.4.4.1 Rejected Comparison


To exercise the failure path, change max_ratio in the reference file to 1.0 and repeat the same command. The measured ratio now exceeds the upper bound, producing exit code 1. The extracted netlist and the comparison remain available to inspect.


These bounds illustrate the mechanism. Choose a justified acceptance interval for the model, its assumptions and the intended use. Passing an interval does not establish calibration.


A numeric capacitance is in farads, and a string accepts SPICE suffixes. The capacitance must be finite and positive. Ratio bounds are optional, finite and nonnegative, with min_ratio no greater than max_ratio. Bounds are inclusive. Omitting both leaves the result informational. Duplicate references for the same device and unordered terminal pair are rejected.


device and device_class identify the device in the extracted LVS circuit, before schematic renaming. Use the names in device_capacitance_checks or the LVS database. The exported netlist may use different schematic-derived names (Section 6.4.3). Terminal names must match that LVS device class.










7.5 Acting on a Check Result


The different failure policies remain independent:







--check n changes the structural failure policy only. It does not disable a requested device comparison or admittance check. When several checks fail, their problems are retained together in the run result.


The examples above were verified with klayout-pex 0.9.0 and the KLayout Python module 0.30.13. The device example explicitly fixes the halo and fringe scaling. Its numbers document that run, not a calibration target or a promise that later coefficient revisions preserve them.










8 Comparison KPEX/2.5D with MAGIC


The initial goal of KPEX/2.5D is to basically come up with the same results as KPEX/MAGIC.












Note







Notes about this comparison:


    

  • Version Magic 8.3 rev 486 is used, but augmented with debug logging6, which will be shown and discussed for each example.

      

    • The sidewall rows were later halved under an interpretation that has since been corrected. They are historical results, not a reference for MAGIC 8.3.693 or KPEX 0.9.0, which restore the full-pair convention (Section 5.4)
      • 

    • 

  • KPEX/MAGIC halo is set to --magic-halo=100000

      

    • NOTE: the screenshots however were created with --magic-halo=8 to give better illustrations
      • 

    • 

  • KPEX/2.5D halo is set to --halo=100000
    • 

  • The test patterns overlap_shield_same_net_* and plate_20um_x_20um_li1_over_* were compared with MAGIC 8.3.681 without debug logging, so their MAGIC capacitances are given per net pair.

8.8 Test Pattern r_single_wire_li1


GDS: https://github.com/iic-jku/klayout-pex/blob/main/testdata/designs/sky130A/test_patterns/r_single_wire_li1.gds.gz















    

  • Wire length \(L = 9.85\,\mu m\)
    • 

  • Wire height \(H = 0.15\,\mu m\)
    • 

  • Layer is li1
    • 

  • Parasitic Table Coefficient \(R_{coeff}(li1) = 12800\,mΩ\)
    • 



If we apply the formula illustrated in Section 5.8.1, we get \[
R_{wire} = \frac{L}{H} * R_{coeff}
\] \[
R_{wire} = \frac{9.85\,\mu m}{0.15\,\mu m} * 12800\,mΩ = 8405\dot{3}\,mΩ = 840.5\dot{3}\,Ω
\]

      •

      • 

    • 

  • Design rules:

      

    • Via width: \(viawidth = 0.17\,\mu m\)
      •

      •

If we apply the formula illustrated in Section 5.8.2, we get


\[
n_x = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{w - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


\[
n_x = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{0.17\,\mu m - (0.17 + 2 * 0.0)\,\mu m}{0.17\,\mu m + 0.19\,\mu m}\right\rfloor = 1
\]


\[
n_y = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{h - (viawidth + 2 * border)}{viawidth + spacing}\right\rfloor
\]


\[
n_y = 1 + \left\lfloor\frac{0.17\,\mu m - (0.17 + 2 * 0.0)\,\mu m}{0.17\,\mu m + 0.19\,\mu m}\right\rfloor = 1
\]


\[
R_{via} = \frac{R_{coeff}}{n_x * n_y}   \,\,\,\,\,\,\, \left[\frac{mΩ}{\text{via count}}\right]
\]


\[
R_{via} = \frac{9300\,mΩ}{1 * 1} = 9300\,mΩ = 9.3\,Ω
\]

9 Netlist reduction: Feasibility study




9.1 TICER algorithm: TIme-Constant Equilibration Reduction


This section reviews the original TICER paper (Sheehan 1999), and illustrates the main ideas.


Given \(N\)-terminal star network:


    

  • node \(N\) is the center
    • 

  • terminals labeled from \(0\) to \(N\!-\!1\) (in Figure 36, \(m\) is used instead of \(N\!-\!1\))
    • 

  • each branch, going from the terminal \(T_i\) to \(N\), contains a resistor and a capacitor in parallel
    • 

  • resistor values are given as conductance (easier parallel summation): \(g_{ij}\,\,[\mho]\)
    

    • 

  • capacitances values: \(c_{ij}\,\,[F]\)
    • 








Sum of resistances \(\gamma_N\), and capacitances \(\chi_N\):


\[
\gamma_N = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_{kN}, \quad \chi_N = \sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_{kN}
\tag{1.2}
\]


The time constant \(\tau_N\) of a given node \(N\) then is: \[
\tau_N = \frac{\chi_N}{\gamma_N} = \frac{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} c_{kN}}{\sum_{k=0}^{N-1} g_{kN}}   \tag{1.3}
\]


Basic node elimination idea: Given a desired frequency window, using the time-constants, we can classify nodes into 3 groups: slow / normal / quick. Then we can eliminate slow and quick nodes, as the normal nodes will suffice to preserve the behavior for the frequency window:


RC circuit in Laplace domain: \[
(s \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{G})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{Y} \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{J}  \tag{2.1}
\]


    

  • \(s \in \mathbb{C}\): Complex Frequency
    • 

  • \(\mathbf{C} \in \mathbb{R}^{N-1 \times N-1}\): nodal capacitances
    • 

  • \(\mathbf{G} \in \mathbb{R}^{N-1 \times N-1}\): nodal conductances
    • 

  • \(\mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^{N-1}\): nodal voltages
    • 

  • \(\mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{N-1}\): current sources at the nodes
    • 



This can be written as a block system: \[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{\tilde{Y}} & \mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{y}^T & s\chi_N + \gamma_N
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\tilde{\mathbf{v}} \\
v_N
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\tilde{\mathbf{J}} \\
j_N
\end{bmatrix}
\tag{2.2}
\]












Note







In equation (2.2), Sheehan uses the tilde accent to name the remainder of the matrix \(\mathbf{Y}\) as \(\mathbf{\tilde{Y}}\), when looking only at the last row and column (same principle applies to vector \(\mathbf{v}\) and \(\mathbf{\tilde{v}}\)): \[\begin{equation}
\mathbf{Y} =
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc:c}
y_{11} & y_{12} & \cdots & y_{1,N-1} & y_{1N} \\
y_{21} & y_{22} & \cdots & y_{2,N-1} & y_{2N} \\
\vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots   & \vdots \\
\hdashline
y_{N1} & y_{N} & \cdots & y_{N,N-1} & y_{NN}
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{c:c}
\mbox{\LARGE $\mathbf{\tilde{Y}}$} &
\begin{array}{c}
y_{1N} \\
y_{2N} \\
\vdots
\end{array} \\ \hdashline
\begin{array}{cccc}
y_{N1} & y_{N2} & \cdots & y_{N,N-1}
\end{array}
&
y_{NN}
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{c:c}
\mbox{\LARGE $\mathbf{\tilde{Y}}$} &
\mbox{\LARGE $\mathbf{y}$} \\ \hdashline
\mbox{\LARGE $\mathbf{y}^T$}
&
y_{NN}
\end{array}
\right]
\end{equation}\]








9.1.1 Comments on page 2, equation \((2.3)\)


To arrive at equations (2.3), (2.4), and (2.5) from equation (2.2), the process involves solving for \(v_N\), the voltage at the node to be eliminated (node \(N\)), and substituting it back into the system of equations.


Starting with equation (2.2):


\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\mathbf{\tilde{Y}} & \mathbf{y} \\
\mathbf{y}^T & s\chi_N + \gamma_N
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\tilde{\mathbf{v}} \\
v_N
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\tilde{\mathbf{J}} \\
j_N
\end{bmatrix}
\tag{2.2}
\]


we have two block equations:


\[
   \mathbf{\tilde{Y}} \tilde{\mathbf{v}} + \mathbf{y} v_N = \tilde{\mathbf{J}}
\tag{\small First block equation of 2.2}
\]


\[
   \mathbf{y}^T \tilde{\mathbf{v}} + (s\chi_N + \gamma_N) v_N = j_N
\tag{\small Second block equation of 2.2}
\]


Solve the second block equation for \(v_N\): \[
   v_N = \frac{j_N - \mathbf{y}^T \tilde{\mathbf{v}}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
   \]


Substitute the expression for \(v_N\) in the first block equation:


\[
   \mathbf{\tilde{Y}} \tilde{\mathbf{v}} + \mathbf{y} \left(\frac{j_N - \mathbf{y}^T \tilde{\mathbf{v}}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}\right) = \tilde{\mathbf{J}}
   \] Simplifying, we get: \[
   \left(\mathbf{\tilde{Y}} - \frac{\mathbf{y} \mathbf{y}^T}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}\right) \tilde{\mathbf{v}} = \tilde{\mathbf{J}} - \frac{\mathbf{y} j_N}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
   \]


This leads to the modified system: \[
(\tilde{Y} - \mathbf{E}) \tilde{\mathbf{v}} = \tilde{\mathbf{J}} - \mathbf{F}
\tag{2.3}
\]


Where:


\[
\mathbf{E} = \frac{\mathbf{y} \mathbf{y}^T}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
\]


\[
\mathbf{F} = \frac{\mathbf{y} j_N}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
\]












Note







There’s a typo in the original paper in (2.3), the printed variable \(\mathbf{v_N}\) should instead be \(\mathbf{\tilde{v}}\).






So we arrive at: \[
\mathbf{E}_{ij} = \frac{(g_{iN} + s c_{iN})(g_{jN} + s c_{jN})}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
\tag{2.4}
\] \[
\mathbf{F}_{i} = \frac{g_{iN} + s c_{iN}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N} j_N
\tag{2.5}
\]






9.1.2 Quick Nodes


Suppose:


    

  • we eliminate a quick node \(N\)
    • 

  • \(s\chi_N \ll \gamma_N\)
    • 

  • equivalently, \(|s \tau_N| \ll 1\)
    • 

  • we approximate \(\mathbf{E}_{ij}\) from (2.4)
    • 

  • we eliminate higher-order terms, containing factors like \(s^n\) for \(n \ge 2\)
    • 



\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_{ij} &= \frac{(g_{iN} + s c_{iN})(g_{jN} + s c_{jN})}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N} \\
                &= \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N} + \frac{s \left( g_{jN} c_{iN} + g_{iN} c_{jN} \right)}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N} + \frac{s^2 c_{iN} c_{jN}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
\end{aligned}
\]


\[
\mathbf{E}_{ij} \approx \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{\cancel{s\chi_N} + \gamma_N} + s\frac{g_{jN} c_{iN} +  g_{iN} c_{jN}}{\cancel{s\chi_N} + \gamma_N} + \cancel{\frac{s^2 c_{iN} c_{jN}}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}}
\]


\[
\mathbf{E}_{ij} \approx \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{\gamma_N} + s\frac{g_{jN} c_{iN} +  g_{iN} c_{jN}}{\gamma_N}   \tag{3.2}
\]


Eliminating a quick node:


Recipe for translating (3.2) into a modified circuit:


    

  • remove all resistors and capacitors connecting other nodes to \(N\)
    • 

  • insert new resistors and capacitors between former neighbors \(i\), \(j\) of \(N\) according to these rules:

      

    • If nodes \(i\) and \(j\) had been connected to \(N\) through conductances \(g_{iN}\) and \(g_{jN}\), insert conductance \(\frac{g_{iN} g_{jN}}{\gamma_N}\) between \(i\) and \(j\)
      • 

    • If node \(i\) had a capacitor \(c_{iN}\) to \(N\), and node \(j\) had a conductance \(g_{jN}\) to \(N\), insert a capacitor \(\frac{c_{iN} g_{jN}}{\gamma_N}\) between \(i\) and \(j\)
      • 

    • 







9.1.3 Slow Nodes


Suppose:


    

  • we eliminate a slow node \(N\)
    • 

  • \(s\chi_N \gg \gamma_N\)
    • 

  • equivalently, \(|s \tau_N| \gg 1\)
    • 

  • we approximate \(\mathbf{E}_{ij}\) from (2.4)
    • 

  • we retain terms containing \(s\)
    • 

  • to preserve DC characteristics, we use \(\frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{\gamma_N}\) in place of whatever constant terms come from the equation
    • 

  • higher-order terms in \(\gamma_N\) and \(s\) are neglected to simplify the expression.
    • 



Starting with (2.4):


\[
\mathbf{E}_{ij} = \frac{(g_{iN} + s c_{iN})(g_{jN} + s c_{jN})}{s\chi_N + \gamma_N}
\tag{2.4}
\]


Given the approximation:


\[
\frac{1}{s \chi_N + \gamma_N} \approx \frac{1}{s \chi_N} \left( 1 - \frac{\gamma_N}{s \chi_N} \right)
\tag{4.2}
\]


Substitute (4.2) into (2.4):


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_{ij} &\approx \frac{(g_{iN} + s c_{iN})(g_{jN} + s c_{jN})}{s\chi_N}\left(1 - \frac{\gamma_N}{s\chi_N}\right) \\
                &\approx \left(\frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{s\chi_N} + \frac{\cancel{s} \left( g_{jN} c_{iN} + g_{iN} c_{jN} \right)}{\cancel{s}\chi_N} + \frac{s\cancel{^2} c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\cancel{s}\chi_N}\right)\left(1 - \frac{\gamma_N}{s\chi_N}\right) \\
\end{aligned}
\]


Expand:


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_{ij} &= \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{s\chi_N} - \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN} \gamma_N}{s^2 \chi_N^2} \\
                &+ \frac{g_{jN} c_{iN} + g_{iN} c_{jN}}{\chi_N} - \frac{\left( g_{jN} c_{iN} + g_{iN} c_{jN} \right) \gamma_N}{s\chi_N^2} \\
                &+ \frac{s c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\chi_N} - \frac{\cancel{s} c_{iN} c_{jN} \gamma_N}{\cancel{s}\chi_N^2}
\end{aligned}
\]


After we remove constant terms:


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_{ij} &\approx \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{s\chi_N} - \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN} \gamma_N}{s^2 \chi_N^2} - \frac{\left( g_{jN} c_{iN} + g_{iN} c_{jN} \right) \gamma_N}{s\chi_N^2} + s \frac{c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\chi_N}
\end{aligned}
\]


Remove higher-order terms in \(\gamma_N\) and \(s\):


\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{E}_{ij} &\approx \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{s\chi_N} + s \frac{c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\chi_N}
\end{aligned}
\]


Sheehan arrives at (4.1):


\[
\mathbf{E}_{ij} \approx \frac{g_{iN}g_{jN}}{\gamma_N} + s\frac{c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\chi_N}
\tag{4.1}
\]


    

  • Rules:

      

    • If nodes \(i\) and \(j\) had been connected to \(N\) through conductances \(g_{iN}\) and \(g_{jN}\), insert conductance \(\frac{g_{iN} g_{jN}}{\gamma_N}\) from \(i\) to \(j\)
      • 

    • If node \(i\) had a capacitor \(c_{iN}\) to \(N\), and node \(j\) had a capacitor \(c_{jN}\) to \(N\), insert a capacitor \(\frac{c_{iN} c_{jN}}{\gamma_N}\) from \(i\) to \(j\)
      • 

    • 









9.2 TICER 2007 paper: Pseudocode


This section reviews some aspects of the 2007 TICER paper (Sheehan 2007).


User-supplied algorithm parameters:


    

  • Set of \(\mathbf{fixed}\) nodes (designated to be left alone, i.e., not to be eliminated)
    • 

  • \(\mathbf{MaxDeg} \in \mathbb{N}\!\setminus\!\{0, 1\}\): number of passes (user-supplied parameter)
    • 

  • \(f^{\text{max}}\): maximum operating frequency of interest
    • 

  • \(\epsilon \in \mathbb{R}_{[0,1]}\): small number enforcing the requirement that \(|s \tau_N| \ll 1\)
    • 



In the paper, figure 5 and 6 demonstrate the algorithm for eliminating a quick node (here is a python conversion of those).


def eliminate_quick_node(N: Node):
   neighbors = nodes_incident_to(node=N)
   for i in neighbors:
      g_iN = conductance[i, N]
      if g_iN == 0: 
         continue
      for j in neighbors:
         if i <= j:
            continue
         g_jN = conductance[j, N]
         c_jN = capacitance[j, N]
         gamma_N = incident_conductance_sum(node=N)
         if g_jN > 0:
            add_conductance(i, j, g_iN * g_jN / gamma_N)
         if c_jN > 0:
            add_capacitance(i, j, g_iN * c_jN / gamma_N)
   remove_all_incident_conductances_and_capacitances(i, N)


def ticer(freq_max: float, epsilon: float, max_deg: int):
   for deg in range(2, max_deg):
      Q = queue.Queue(nodes_not_fixed())
      while not Q.empty():
         N = Q.get()  # pop
         if number_of_incident_resistors(N) > deg:
            continue
         tau_N = time_constant(N)
         if 2 * math.pi * freq_max * tau_N <= epsilon:
            # ensure the neighbors are in the queue,
            # because the neighbors' incident resistors and time constants 
            # might have been changed, so they should be reconsidered for elimination
            missing_neighbors = [n in nodes_incident_to(node=N) if n not in Q]
            q.push(missing_neighbors)

            eliminate_quick_node(N)

   # NOTE: "leaf node" N means, number_of_incident_resistors(N) == 1
   for N in leaf_nodes():
      if N in fixed_nodes():  # N is protected
         continue

      tau_N = time_constant(N)
      if 2 * math.pi * freq_max * tau_N <= epsilon:
         eliminate_quick_node(N)




9.2.1 Pseudocode for slow node elimination


Sheehan mentions that elimination of slow nodes is of reduced importances, and therefore does not explicitly provide pseudocode for this case, instead refers to the original TICER paper (Sheehan 1999).


So if we fill in the gaps we arrive at:


def eliminate_slow_node(N: Node):
   neighbors = nodes_incident_to(node=N)
   for i in neighbors:
      g_iN = conductance[i, N]
      c_iN = capacitance[i, N]
      for j in neighbors:
         if i <= j:
            continue
         g_jN = conductance[j, N]
         c_jN = capacitance[j, N]
         gamma_N = incident_conductance_sum(node=N)
         if g_iN > 0 and g_jN > 0:
            add_conductance(i, j, g_iN * g_jN / gamma_N)
         if c_iN > 0 and c_jN > 0:
            add_capacitance(i, j, c_iN * c_jN / gamma_N)
   remove_all_incident_conductances_and_capacitances(i, N)


To integrate this into the algorithm, we additionally need a minimum frequency \(f^{\text{min}}\) parameter supplied by the user.


def ticer(freq_min: float, freq_max: float, epsilon: float, max_deg: int):
   for deg in range(2, max_deg):
      Q = queue.Queue(nodes_not_fixed())
      while not Q.empty():
         N = Q.get()  # pop
         if number_of_incident_resistors(N) > deg:
            continue
         tau_N = time_constant(N)
         if 2 * math.pi * freq_max * tau_N <= epsilon:
            # NOTE: ensure the neighbors are in the queue,
            # because the neighbors' incident resistors and time constants 
            # might have been changed, so they should be reconsidered for elimination
            missing_neighbors = [n in nodes_incident_to(node=N) if n not in Q]
            q.push(missing_neighbors)

            eliminate_quick_node(N)

         if 2 * math.pi * freq_min * tau_N <= epsilon:
            # NOTE: ensure the neighbors are in the queue,
            # because the neighbors' incident resistors and time constants 
            # might have been changed, so they should be reconsidered for elimination
            missing_neighbors = [n in nodes_incident_to(node=N) if n not in Q]
            q.push(missing_neighbors)

            eliminate_slow_node(N)

   # NOTE: "leaf node" N means, number_of_incident_resistors(N) == 1
   for N in leaf_nodes():
      if N in fixed_nodes():  # N is protected
         continue

      tau_N = time_constant(N)
      if 2 * math.pi * freq_max * tau_N <= epsilon:
         eliminate_quick_node(N)








9.3 Example from TICER 2007 paper


Let’s reduce the example presented by Sheehan in the from the 2007 paper (Sheehan 2007), as shown in Figure 37. The goal is to eliminate the quick node \(v_3\).















    

  • Time constant \(\tau_{v_3} = \frac{c_3}{g_{13} + g_{23}}\)
    • 

  • Quick node condition: \(\text{is\_quick}(N) := 2 \pi f^{\text{max}} \tau_N < \epsilon\)
    • 



Elimination of node \(N_2\):


    

  • Incident devices \(R_{13}\), \(R_{23}\), \(C_{3}\) are removed
    • 

  • New devices for neighbors

      

    • Between nodes \((v_0, v_1)\):

        

      • add \(c_{10} = \frac{g_{13}*c_{3}}{g_{13} + g_{23}}\)
        • 

      • 

    • Between nodes \((v_0, v_2)\):

        

      • add \(c_{20} = \frac{g_{23}*c_{3}}{g_{13} + g_{23}}\)
        • 

      • 

    • Between nodes \((v_1, v_2)\):

        

      • add \(g_{12} = \frac{g_{13}*g_{23}}{g_{13} + g_{23}}\)
        • 

      • 

    • 


















9.3.1 Modified Nodal Analysis in the Laplace domain


RC circuit in Laplace domain:


\[
(s \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{G})\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{Y} \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{J}  \tag{2.1}
\]


Solve for voltages:


\[
\mathbf{v} = (s \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{G})^{-1} \mathbf{J} = Y^{-1} \mathbf{J}
\]


Transfer function:


\[
H(s) = \frac{\mathbf{v}(s)}{\mathbf{J}(s)} = Y^{-1}(s) = (s \mathbf{G} + \mathbf{C})^{-1}
\]


E.g. the transfer function (for input \(J_1(s)\), output \(V_2(s)\)) is:


\[
H(s) = \frac{\text{adj}(s \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{G})_{21}}{det(s \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{G})}
\]






9.3.2 Analysis of the original circuit


So for the original circuit of Figure 37, we have 3 nodes, in addition to GND (\(v_0\)).


So we have 3 nodal equations:


\[
\begin{aligned}
c_1 \dot{v_1} + g_d v_1 + g_{13} (v_1 - v_3)              &= j_1(t) \\
c_2 \dot{v_2} + g_{23} (v_2 - v_3)                        &= 0      \\
c_3 \dot{v_3} + g_{13} (v_3 - v_1) + g_{23} * (v_3 - v_2) &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]


Laplace domain (MNA8 form):


\[
\left(
s
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
c_1 &   0 &   0 \\
  0 & c_2 &   0 \\
  0 &   0 & c_3
\end{array}
\right]
+
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
g_d + g_{13}  &        0 & -g_{13}         \\
0             &   g_{23} & -g_{23}         \\
-g_{13}       &  -g_{23} & g_{13} + g_{23}
\end{array}
\right]
\right)
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
V_{1}(s) \\
V_{2}(s) \\
V_{3}(s)
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
J_{1}(s) \\
0 \\
0
\end{array}
\right]
\]


So given the values from Sheehan’s numerical example:


    

  • \(g_d = g_{13} = g_{23} = 1\)
    • 

  • \(c_1 = c_2 = 1\)
    • 

  • \(c_3 = 0.01\)
    • 



Node \(v_3\) is a quick node:


    

  • Time constant: \(\tau_{v_3} = \frac{c_3}{g_{13} + g_{23}} = \frac{0.001}{1 + 1} = 0.0005\)
    • 

  • Frequency: \(f = \frac{1}{2 \pi \tau_{v_3}} \approx 318.31\,\text{Hz}\)
    • 



We have a system with \[
\mathbf{C} =
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
  1 &   0 &    0 \\
  0 &   1 &    0 \\
  0 &   0 & 0.01
\end{array}
\right],
\mathbf{G} =
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
   2 &   0 & -1 \\
   0 &   1 & -1 \\
  -1 &  -1 &  2
\end{array}
\right]
\]


Transfer function:


\[
H(s) = \frac{1}{0.01s^3 + 2.03s^2 + 4.02s + 1}
\]






9.3.3 Analysis of the reduced circuit


The reduced circuit in Figure 38 only has 2 remaining nodes (besides GND).


So we have 2 nodal equations:


\[
\begin{aligned}
(c_1 + c_{10}) \dot{v_1} + g_d v_1 + g_{12} (v_1 - v_2)   &= j_1(t) \\
(c_2 + c_{20}) \dot{v_2} + g_{12} (v_2 - v_1)             &= 0
\end{aligned}
\]


Laplace domain (MNA9 form):


\[
\left(
s
\left[
\begin{array}{cc}
c_1 + c_{10} &            0 \\
           0 & c_2 + c_{20}
\end{array}
\right]
+
\left[
\begin{array}{cccc}
g_d + g_{12}  & -g_{12}         \\
-g_{12}       &  g_{12}
\end{array}
\right]
\right)
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
V_{1}(s) \\
V_{2}(s)
\end{array}
\right]
=
\left[
\begin{array}{c}
J_{1}(s) \\
0
\end{array}
\right]
\]


New devices:


    

  • \(c_{10} = \frac{g_{13}*c_{3}}{g_{13} + g_{23}} = \frac{1 * 0.01}{1 + 1} = 0.005\)
    • 

  • \(c_{20} = \frac{g_{23}*c_{3}}{g_{13} + g_{23}} = \frac{1 * 0.01}{1 + 1} = 0.005\)
    • 

  • \(g_{12} = \frac{g_{13}*g_{23}}{g_{13} + g_{23}} = \frac{1 * 1}{1 + 1} = 0.5\)
    • 



We have a system with:


\[
\mathbf{C} =
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
1.005 &   0  \\
  0 & 1.005  
\end{array}
\right],
\mathbf{G} =
\left[
\begin{array}{ccc}
    1.5 &  -0.5 \\
   -0.5 &  0.5
\end{array}
\right]
\]


Transfer function:


\[
H(s) = \frac{0.5}{1.010025s^2 + 2.01s + 0.5}
\]
